# Because I Could Not Stop for Death analysis

Because I Could Not Stop for Death — Emily Dickinson (1890)

Emily Dickinson's Because I Could Not Stop for Death turns dying into a calm carriage ride with a courteous but unsettling companion. This analysis follows the poem's movement from ordinary life through the grave toward an uncertain eternity.

## The poem

```
Because I could not stop for Death—
He kindly stopped for me—
The Carriage held but just Ourselves—
And Immortality.

We slowly drove—He knew no haste
And I had put away
My labor and my leisure too,
For His Civility—

We passed the School, where Children strove
At Recess—in the Ring—
We passed the Fields of Gazing Grain—
We passed the Setting Sun—

Or rather—He passed Us—
The Dews drew quivering and chill—
For only Gossamer, my Gown—
My Tippet—only Tulle—

We paused before a House that seemed
A Swelling of the Ground—
The Roof was scarcely visible—
The Cornice—in the Ground—

Since then—’tis Centuries—and yet
Feels shorter than the Day
I first surmised the Horses’ Heads
Were toward Eternity—
```

Text from [Because I could not stop for Death — Academy of American Poets](https://poets.org/poem/because-i-could-not-stop-death-479). Public domain in the US (First published posthumously in the United States in 1890; the poem and its 1890 publication are public domain in the United States.).

## Summary

The speaker is too occupied to stop for Death, but Death courteously stops for her. She enters a carriage with Death and Immortality, gives up both work and leisure, and travels past children, grain, and the setting sun.

The journey changes when the speaker realizes that the sun—or Death—has passed them and that she is inadequately dressed for the cold. The carriage pauses at a grave described as a house in the ground; centuries later, the speaker still remembers first guessing that the horses were headed toward Eternity.

## Meaning and interpretation

Death appears as a courteous suitor, but the politeness is not wholly reassuring. “Kindly” and “Civility” make the journey sound like a genteel visit while also showing how completely the speaker yields control: she puts away both labor and leisure and accepts Death's pace.

The poem does not settle whether Immortality is a promised destination, a silent passenger, or an expectation that remains unresolved. The final “toward Eternity” is directional rather than conclusive, so the afterlife remains mysterious even after the speaker has spent centuries beyond the grave.

## Themes

### Death as a social encounter

Personified Death behaves like a patient gentleman caller who offers a carriage and observes formal civility. The calm manners make death familiar, but they can also make the speaker's surrender feel like an abduction disguised as courtesy.

### The stages of life

The carriage passes a school, fields of grain, and the setting sun. These images suggest childhood, productive maturity, and life's decline, compressing a whole life into a slow route toward the grave.

### Immortality and uncertainty

Immortality rides in the carriage but never speaks. Its presence suggests survival beyond death without proving what that survival means; the last movement toward Eternity preserves that uncertainty.

### The grave as a house

The grave is rendered through domestic architecture: a roof, a cornice, and a house that swells from the ground. The familiar vocabulary makes burial seem like habitation while the buried structure remains stark and Gothic.

## Form and meter

The poem has six quatrains and is commonly described as using common meter, the hymn-like alternation of iambic tetrameter and trimeter. Dickinson varies the pattern through pauses, substitutions, and slant rhyme.

The carriage's slow motion is reinforced by repeated “We passed” phrasing and the poem's measured quatrains. The fourth stanza interrupts the comfortable progress: cold dew and fragile clothing expose the physical danger beneath the courteous surface.

End rhyme is often approximate rather than exact: “me” and “Immortality,” “away” and “Civility,” and “Day” and “Eternity” create echoes without fully closing the sound.

## Literary devices

### Personification

> He kindly stopped for me—

Death acts as a courteous driver and companion. Giving Death human manners makes an abstract event narratable while keeping the speaker's relationship to it emotionally ambiguous.

### Extended metaphor

> The Carriage held but just Ourselves— / And Immortality.

The carriage ride sustains the poem's central model for dying: departure, passage, arrival at the grave, and a possible continuation toward Eternity.

### Symbolic imagery

> We passed the School ... / The Fields of Gazing Grain—

School, grain, and the setting sun form a compressed sequence of human development and decline. The journey's outward scenery becomes a map of time.

### Paradox and reversal

> Or rather—He passed Us—

The correction changes the apparent direction of the journey. It also unsettles the speaker's control over perception: what seemed to be a passage past the sun becomes a passage in which Death or time overtakes them.

## Historical context

The poem was written around 1862 and first published posthumously in Poems by Emily Dickinson in 1890, edited by Mabel Loomis Todd and Thomas Wentworth Higginson. The 1890 volume titled it “The Chariot,” omitted the fourth stanza, and regularized aspects of Dickinson's punctuation and wording.

The restored reading text includes the fourth stanza and Dickinson's distinctive capitalization and dashes. The Academy of American Poets notes that Dickinson was not publicly recognized during her lifetime and that the first volume of her poetry appeared after her death in 1886.

## What critics say

> “For many modern readers, the omitted fourth stanza is the emotional heart of the poem and its turning point.”
>
> — Cristanne Miller, [White Heat, Dartmouth College](https://journeys.dartmouth.edu/whiteheat/jan8-14f479/)

> “The poem becomes a satiric portrait of Victorian gentility and repression …”
>
> — Cristanne Miller, [White Heat, Dartmouth College](https://journeys.dartmouth.edu/whiteheat/jan8-14f479/)

## Common questions

### What is the main meaning of Because I Could Not Stop for Death?

The poem imagines death as a calm carriage ride that moves through the stages of life, pauses at a grave, and continues toward an uncertain Eternity. Its polite tone does not remove the ambiguity or vulnerability of dying.

### Why is Death described as a courteous suitor?

Death “kindly” stops for the speaker and drives without haste, using the manners of a gentleman caller. That courtesy makes death approachable, but it also suggests that the speaker is being persuaded or carried away rather than freely choosing the journey.

### What does the house in the ground represent?

The house is a grave. Calling it a house makes burial sound like entering a dwelling, while the barely visible roof and cornice keep the image materially unsettling and emphasize how fully the speaker is being covered by the earth.

### What meter does the poem use?

It is commonly read as common meter, alternating roughly between four-beat and three-beat lines, like a hymn. Dickinson varies the rhythm and rhyme, so the pattern is audible without being rigid.

## References

- [Because I could not stop for Death — full poem](https://poets.org/poem/because-i-could-not-stop-death-479) — Academy of American Poets

- [Because I could not / stop for Death — textual history and criticism](https://journeys.dartmouth.edu/whiteheat/jan8-14f479/) — Dartmouth College, White Heat

- [The Chariot — 1890 first-series text](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/12242/12242-h/12242-h.htm) — Project Gutenberg

## Open the editor

# Bless God, he went as soldiers analysis

Bless God, he went as soldiers — Emily Dickinson (1890)

This analysis explains how Emily Dickinson uses a soldier’s imagined afterlife to connect faith with courage. Explore the poem’s meaning, themes, form, and imagery.

## The poem

```
BLESS God, he went as soldiers,
His musket on his breast;
Grant, God, he charge the bravest
Of all the martial blest.

Please God, might I behold him
In epauletted white,
I should not fear the foe then,
I should not fear the fight.
```

Text from [Bless God, he went as soldiers](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Poems:_Third_Series/Bless_God,_he_went_as_soldiers). Public domain in the US (First published posthumously in the United States in Poems, Third Series in 1896, the poem is in the US public domain.).

## Summary

The speaker imagines a beloved man entering battle with his musket on his breast and asks God to make him one of the bravest among the blessed. Military language turns death or spiritual struggle into a scene of enlistment and promotion.

In the second stanza, the speaker asks to see the man transformed into “epauletted white,” a figure who is both decorated soldier and angelic presence. Seeing that vision would give the speaker courage to face an unnamed foe and fight.

## Meaning and interpretation

The poem’s central meaning lies in its conditional structure: the speaker says she would not fear the foe or fight if she could behold the beloved in a confirmed heavenly state. Faith is therefore desired but not fully possessed; the speaker asks for an image that would make courage possible.

Dickinson leaves the foe and fight unspecified. They may suggest death, spiritual evil, grief, or a literal future conflict, but the omission keeps the poem focused on the speaker’s need for assurance rather than on a named enemy.

The movement from musket to white epaulettes joins earthly martial identity to heavenly reward. The soldier’s bravery is not presented as proof the speaker already has; it is something she asks God to grant and reveal.

## Themes

### Faith and uncertainty

Repeated appeals to God—“Bless,” “Grant,” and “Please”—make belief sound like a request awaiting an answer. The speaker wants visible confirmation before she can claim confidence.

### Courage through an example

The beloved soldier becomes the source of the speaker’s possible bravery. If she can see him honored in white, his courage will let her face her own unnamed battle.

### War and spiritual language

Musket, charge, martial, foe, and fight create a military vocabulary, while “blest,” “God,” and white clothing move the scene toward Christian afterlife imagery.

## Form and meter

The poem has two quatrains. Its short lines broadly resemble common meter, alternating longer and shorter lines in a hymn-like pattern, though Dickinson’s stresses and phrasing make the rhythm flexible.

The first stanza uses an ABCB-like pattern, with “breast” and “blest” as a slant rhyme. The second stanza similarly pairs “white” and “fight,” giving the poem a restrained, hymn-shaped closure.

The compact quatrains and repeated end sounds make the speaker’s prayers feel formal, while the abrupt syntax keeps the emotional situation unresolved.

## Literary devices

### Extended martial metaphor

> His musket on his breast;

The poem describes spiritual or posthumous status through the language of a soldier’s enlistment, charge, rank, and battle.

### Imagery

> In epauletted white,

The visual image combines military insignia with the whiteness associated with angels or heavenly purity. The speaker wants to see this image, not merely hear an argument about it.

### Anaphora

> Bless God ... / Grant, God ... / Please God ...

The repeated address to God creates a prayer-like rhythm and emphasizes the speaker’s dependence on divine confirmation.

### Conditional syntax

> I should not fear the foe then—

The word “then” makes courage dependent on a future vision. The speaker’s confidence remains hypothetical rather than complete.

## Historical context

Dickinson preserved the poem in an early fascicle, around 1859. It was later published posthumously in Poems, Third Series in 1896, where it appeared as poem XX.

Because it predates the American Civil War, its military vocabulary should not automatically be reduced to a response to that later conflict.

The poem’s historical setting still matters: nineteenth-century Christian and military ideals overlap in its image of a brave soldier becoming one of the “martial blest.” The unnamed foe and fight allow the poem to move between literal war, death, and inner struggle.

## What critics say

> “The larger consequence of these efforts is to show, once and for all, that Dickinson was never isolated from the world, but rather sensitively engaged with local and national events.”
>
> — Maya C. Popa, [Maya C. Popa, “Eternity Only Will Answer,” Poetry Foundation](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/articles/162413/eternity-only-will-answer)

> “Yet there is no resolution in the poem, she does not see the soldier “In [his] epauletted white” ... She wants proof, but God remains silent all through the poem.”
>
> — [BookishNerDan, “Bless God, he went as soldiers”](https://slowlander.com/2019/06/07/page-45-of-864-of-emily-dickinsons-poems-as-she-preserved-them-2/)

## Common questions

### What is the meaning of “Bless God, he went as soldiers”?

The speaker imagines a beloved soldier in heaven and asks to see him honored there. That vision would give her the courage to face an unnamed foe and fight.

### What does “epauletted white” mean?

The phrase combines a soldier’s decorated shoulders with heavenly white clothing. The beloved appears as both honored military figure and angelic presence.

### What are the main themes of the poem?

The main themes are faith and uncertainty, courage gained from another person’s example, and the overlap between military and spiritual language.

### What is the form and meter of the poem?

It consists of two quatrains in a flexible hymn-like pattern that broadly resembles common meter. Slant rhymes such as “breast” and “blest” support its restrained, prayerful sound.

## References

- [Bless God, he went as soldiers](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Poems:_Third_Series/Bless_God,_he_went_as_soldiers) — Wikisource

- [Emily Dickinson’s Prewar Martial Poems](https://hit-u.repo.nii.ac.jp/records/2042924) — Hitotsubashi University Repository

## Open the editor

Write with this poem’s meter in the editor: https://lyriic.com/write

# Chicago analysis

Chicago — Carl Sandburg (1914)

Carl Sandburg’s “Chicago” answers the city’s critics by admitting its violence, poverty, and corruption before celebrating its work, pride, and vitality. Read the full poem with an analysis of its free verse, imagery, rhetoric, and historical setting.

## The poem

```
Hog Butcher for the World,

Tool Maker, Stacker of Wheat,

Player with Railroads and the Nation's Freight Handler;

Stormy, husky, brawling,

City of the Big Shoulders:

They tell me you are wicked and I believe them, for I have seen your painted women under the gas lamps luring the farm boys.

And they tell me you are crooked and I answer: Yes, it is true I have seen the gunman kill and go free to kill again.

And they tell me you are brutal and my reply is: On the faces of women and children I have seen the marks of wanton hunger.

And having answered so I turn once more to those who sneer at this my city, and I give them back the sneer and say to them:

Come and show me another city with lifted head singing so proud to be alive and coarse and strong and cunning.

Flinging magnetic curses amid the toil of piling job on job, here is a tall bold slugger set vivid against the little soft cities;

Fierce as a dog with tongue lapping for action, cunning as a savage pitted against the wilderness,

Bareheaded,

Shoveling,

Wrecking,

Planning,

Building, breaking, rebuilding,

Under the smoke, dust all over his mouth, laughing with white teeth,

Under the terrible burden of destiny laughing as a young man laughs,

Laughing even as an ignorant fighter laughs who has never lost a battle,

Bragging and laughing that under his wrist is the pulse, and under his ribs the heart of the people,

Laughing!

Laughing the stormy, husky, brawling laughter of Youth, half-naked, sweating, proud to be Hog Butcher, Tool Maker, Stacker of Wheat, Player with Railroads and Freight Handler to the Nation.
```

Text from [Chicago](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poetrymagazine/poems/12840/chicago). Public domain in the US (First published in Poetry magazine in March 1914, Chicago is in the public domain in the United States.).

## Summary

The speaker names Chicago through its industrial roles, then acknowledges the city’s reputation for vice, crime, and hunger.

After conceding those charges, the speaker turns the defense outward. Chicago becomes a powerful worker—shoveling, wrecking, planning, and rebuilding—whose laughter expresses resilient civic pride.

## Meaning and interpretation

The poem’s defense is persuasive because it does not pretend Chicago is innocent. The speaker has seen its harms, but argues that honesty about those harms can coexist with admiration for the city’s energy and people.

Sandburg makes labor the measure of Chicago’s greatness. The city is imagined as a sweating, bareheaded young man whose strength comes from collective work rather than polished manners or inherited prestige.

## Themes

### Industrial labor and dignity

The opening catalog identifies Chicago through work: slaughtering, making tools, stacking grain, and moving freight. The closing gathers those jobs into a proud identity, giving labor a central place in the city’s self-image.

### Pride with clear eyes

The speaker admits prostitution, murder, and hunger before praising Chicago. That double vision keeps the poem from becoming simple civic propaganda: its pride is built on seeing the city’s damage as well as its power.

### Youth and resilience

The repeated laughter turns hardship into motion and defiance. Chicago is young, rough, and unfinished, but its ability to keep building and rebuilding becomes a form of hope.

## Form and meter

“Chicago” is free verse: it has no fixed stanza pattern, end-rhyme scheme, or regular metrical line. Its shape comes from sentence movement, catalogues, punctuation, and dramatic shifts in line length.

The middle section uses repeated syntax—“And they tell me…”—to create an accusation-and-answer structure. The speaker concedes each charge, then pivots toward a challenge to the cities that sneer at Chicago.

Short one-word lines such as “Bareheaded,” “Shoveling,” and “Laughing!” interrupt the long rushing sentences. They work like drumbeats or snapshots of physical action, while the final accumulation returns to the poem’s opening occupational titles.

## Literary devices

### Personification

> “here is a tall bold slugger”

Chicago becomes a single working body: a fighter with a mouth, wrist, ribs, sweat, and laughter. Personification makes the city’s economic activity feel physical and emotionally alive.

### Catalog and anaphora

> “And they tell me you are…”

Lists of occupations and repeated sentence openings give the poem an expansive, public voice. The catalogue suggests that no single image can contain the city; its identity is made from many kinds of work and conflict.

### Simile

> “Fierce as a dog with tongue lapping for action”

The animal comparison emphasizes appetite, alertness, and readiness. It presents Chicago’s roughness as a source of energy rather than something to be hidden.

### Repetition and sound

> “Laughing… / Laughing… / Laughing!”

The repeated word gathers force as the poem closes. Hard consonants in “stormy, husky, brawling” and the recurring occupational names make the ending sound like a chant or public boast.

## Historical context

Sandburg moved to Chicago in 1912 and worked as a reporter, where he encountered unsafe working conditions, labor inequities, and the city’s rapidly industrializing life. Those concerns help explain why the poem treats work and social harm as inseparable parts of Chicago’s identity.

Harriet Monroe published “Chicago” in the March 1914 issue of Poetry magazine and awarded Sandburg the Levinson Prize for the poem. It later appeared in Sandburg’s 1916 collection Chicago Poems.

The poem’s “Hog Butcher,” grain, railroads, and freight imagery reflects Chicago’s role as a major industrial and transportation center. Sandburg turns that economic reality into a portrait of a city that is powerful precisely because it is active, unfinished, and human.

## What critics say

> ““Chicago” became one of the best known works of 20th century American literature.”
>
> — U.S. National Park Service, [Carl Sandburg Home National Historic Site](https://www.nps.gov/carl/learn/historyculture/chicago.htm)

> “Source: Poetry (March 1914)”
>
> — [Poetry Foundation](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poetrymagazine/poems/12840/chicago)

## Common questions

### What is the main meaning of “Chicago”?

The poem celebrates Chicago’s industrial strength and working people without denying its crime, poverty, and corruption. Sandburg argues that the city’s rough vitality and resilience are part of its truth.

### Why does Sandburg call Chicago the “City of the Big Shoulders”?

The phrase personifies Chicago as a strong laborer. Its “big shoulders” suggest the physical work, industrial capacity, and collective burden that support the city.

### What form does “Chicago” use?

“Chicago” is a free-verse poem with no fixed meter or rhyme scheme. Its rhythm comes from repetition, occupational catalogues, long sentences, short action lines, and the repeated word “Laughing!”

### Is the full text of “Chicago” available in the editor?

Yes. The complete poem is available in lyriic’s local-first editor for reading and analysis; your text stays in the browser rather than being sent to a server.

## References

- [Chicago: poem text and 1914 source](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poetrymagazine/poems/12840/chicago) — Poetry Foundation

- [Chicago: biography and historical context](https://www.nps.gov/carl/learn/historyculture/chicago.htm) — Carl Sandburg Home National Historic Site, National Park Service

# Doubt No More That Oberon analysis

Doubt No More That Oberon — Edna St. Vincent Millay (1921)

This analysis of Edna St. Vincent Millay’s “Doubt No More That Oberon” explores how myth and spring let a speaker argue for wonder in a damaged age.

## The poem

```
Doubt no more that Oberon—
Never doubt that Pan
Lived, and played a reed, and ran
After nymphs in a dark forest,
In the merry, credulous days,—
Lived, and led a fairy band
Over the indulgent land!
Ah, for in this dourest, sorest
Age man’s eye has looked upon,
Death to fauns and death to fays,
Still the dog-wood dares to raise—
Healthy tree, with trunk and root—
Ivory bowls that bear no fruit,
And the starlings and the jays—
Birds that cannot even sing—
Dare to come again in spring!
```

Text from [Second April, full text](https://monadnock.net/millay/). Public domain in the US (First published in Millay’s 1921 collection Second April, this poem is in the public domain in the United States.).

## Summary

The speaker begins by insisting that Oberon and Pan should not be dismissed as childish inventions. The remembered world of nymphs, fairies, and “merry, credulous” belief becomes a counter-image to the present age, described as the most sorrowful one human beings have seen.

The poem’s proof is not a supernatural apparition but ordinary spring. A dogwood tree and commonplace birds return despite their limitations, suggesting that renewal can persist even when beauty is fruitless, songless, or difficult to believe in.

## Meaning and interpretation

The poem means that wonder does not have to survive in its old, ideal form to remain real. Pan’s mythic music is replaced by the stubborn recurrence of trees and birds: imperfect natural life becomes evidence that the world still exceeds the bleakness of its historical moment.

The ending is hopeful without being sentimental. “Ivory bowls that bear no fruit” and birds “that cannot even sing” are deliberately modest signs. Millay does not claim that spring cures mortality; she argues that the act of returning, even without usefulness or magnificence, is itself a form of resistance.

## Themes

### Wonder versus modern despair

The imperative “Doubt no more” answers an age that has lost faith in myth. The poem treats belief as an active choice rather than naïveté.

### Nature’s stubborn renewal

The dogwood, starlings, and jays return in spring without becoming idealized. Their persistence gives the speaker a grounded alternative to vanished fauns and fays.

### Beauty alongside mortality

The poem acknowledges death directly before turning to growth. Its hope is therefore limited and credible: life returns, but it does not erase loss.

## Form and meter

This is a compact, single-stanza lyric of sixteen lines. Its short lines and emphatic imperatives create a chant-like movement, while the uneven line lengths keep the poem from settling into a regular metrical pattern.

The rhyme is audible but irregular: “Pan” echoes “ran,” “days” returns with “fays,” and the final “sing/spring” couplet gives the close a firm sonic resolution. Repeated syntax—especially “Lived” and “Dare”—supplies more structural unity than a fixed stanza pattern.

Because the poem’s rhythm is variable and its lineation carries much of its force, the editor is set to open reading mode rather than a predetermined meter.

## Literary devices

### Mythological allusion

> Never doubt that Pan / Lived, and played a reed

Oberon and Pan invoke European fairy lore and classical nature mythology. Their presence enlarges the poem’s small spring scene into a debate about whether enchantment has disappeared.

### Personification

> Still the dog-wood dares to raise—

The dogwood is given courage and agency. “Dares” makes seasonal growth sound like a deliberate challenge to the age’s despair.

### Paradox and understatement

> Ivory bowls that bear no fruit

The tree’s flowers are beautiful yet unproductive, and the birds return despite being unable to sing. These compromised forms of beauty make the poem’s hope more demanding than a simple celebration of spring.

### Repetition

> Lived ... / Lived ... / Dare ... / Dare ...

The repeated verbs insist on continuance. The poem moves from mythic life to natural recurrence through a series of verbal assertions.

## Historical context

Doubt No More That Oberon appeared in Second April (1921), a collection written in the shadow of personal loss and the 1918 influenza pandemic. The Los Angeles Review of Books describes the collection’s poems as confronting springtime with mortality and notes that contemporary readers found their gloom nearly strong enough to outweigh their lyricism.

Millay’s invocation of Pan belongs to a broader literary conversation about the survival or disappearance of pagan nature figures. In a 1969 essay, Thomas Burnett Swann places Millay among poets who “resurrect” Pan for a modern century estranged from the natural world.

## What critics say

> “These struck an unconventional note. The Vassar Miscellany News would later report that “they breathed a gloom so unmitigated as almost to outweigh their lyrical quality.””
>
> — V.M. Braganza, [Los Angeles Review of Books](https://lareviewofbooks.org/blog/essays/second-april/)

> “But Pan was an insider and not an outsider; he reminds us how it was with the Greeks, when even the largest city was within walking distance of a forest.”
>
> — Thomas Burnett Swann, [WSFA Journal 68](https://fanac.org/fanzines/WSFA_Journal/WSFA_Journal68.pdf)

## Common questions

### What is the meaning of “Doubt No More That Oberon”?

The poem argues that wonder and renewal remain possible even in a deeply sorrowful age. Nature’s imperfect return in spring replaces the lost world of fairy mythology as evidence of persistence.

### What are the main themes in the poem?

Its main themes are wonder versus despair, nature’s renewal, and beauty existing alongside mortality. The poem is hopeful, but its hope is deliberately modest rather than idealized.

### What form does “Doubt No More That Oberon” use?

It is a sixteen-line, single-stanza lyric with irregular meter, short lines, recurring end sounds, and a final “sing/spring” couplet. Its repeated verbs and syntax provide much of its rhythm.

### Who are Oberon and Pan?

Oberon is the fairy king of European literary tradition, while Pan is the Greek god associated with forests, shepherds, music, and the wild. Millay uses both figures to represent an older, more enchanted relationship with nature.

## References

- [Second April, full text and publication listing](https://monadnock.net/millay/) — Monadnock Valley Press

- [Second April in historical context](https://lareviewofbooks.org/blog/essays/second-april/) — Los Angeles Review of Books

- [Pan and His Friends](https://fanac.org/fanzines/WSFA_Journal/WSFA_Journal68.pdf) — WSFA Journal

## Open the editor

# Dreams analysis

Dreams — Langston Hughes (1922)

This analysis explains how Langston Hughes presents dreams as necessary for a life with movement, purpose, and possibility. Explore the poem’s meaning, themes, form, and imagery.

## The poem

```
Hold fast to dreams
For if dreams die
Life is a broken-winged bird
That cannot fly.

Hold fast to dreams
For when dreams go
Life is a barren field
Frozen with snow.
```

Text from [Dreams](https://poets.org/poem/dreams). Public domain in the US (The poem is documented as a 1922 work, placing its first publication before the US public-domain cutoff used for this catalog.).

## Summary

The speaker gives a direct command: hold tightly to dreams. Without them, life becomes like a bird with a broken wing—alive, but unable to do what gives it freedom and motion.

The second stanza intensifies the warning. When dreams disappear, life becomes a barren field frozen in snow: sterile, still, and unable to support growth.

## Meaning and interpretation

“Dreams” can mean hopes, aspirations, imaginative visions, or a sense of future possibility. Hughes leaves the word open enough to include both private goals and the larger dreams of communities.

The poem does not describe dreams as optional decoration. Its comparisons suggest that dreams sustain life’s movement and capacity to grow; losing them is presented as a condition of deprivation.

The shift from “if dreams die” to “when dreams go” makes the warning more urgent. Dreams may be vulnerable, so the imperative to “hold fast” asks readers to protect them while they can.

## Themes

### Hope and aspiration

The repeated command treats dreams as the source of a meaningful future. Holding onto them becomes an active form of hope rather than passive wishing.

### Loss and emotional sterility

The broken bird and frozen field turn the absence of dreams into physical conditions: impaired movement first, then complete barrenness and stillness.

### Freedom and possibility

A bird that cannot fly evokes lost freedom, while a field normally associated with cultivation becomes barren. Together, the images show how abandoned dreams restrict both movement and growth.

## Form and meter

The poem is made of two compact quatrains. Each stanza begins with the same imperative, creating a refrain-like structure that makes the advice memorable and urgent.

The short lines are closest to iambic dimeter, though Hughes varies the stresses to keep the language natural and forceful. The compressed rhythm suits the poem’s plainspoken warning.

There is no elaborate end-rhyme scheme. Repetition, parallel syntax, and the echo of “die” / “fly” provide more of the poem’s musical cohesion than a regular rhyme pattern.

## Literary devices

### Extended metaphor

> Life is a broken-winged bird / That cannot fly.

The poem translates the abstract loss of dreams into an injured creature. The bird’s lost ability to fly makes dreamlessness feel painful, limiting, and threatening to survival.

### Metaphor

> Life is a barren field / Frozen with snow.

The field image expands the first comparison from impaired movement to total sterility. Barren ground and freezing weather suggest that no new growth can begin.

### Repetition

> Hold fast to dreams

Repeating the opening command at the start of both stanzas gives the poem the sound of advice or a refrain. It also keeps the central instruction in the foreground.

### Juxtaposition

> if dreams die” / “when dreams go

The poem places the vitality of dreams beside images of death, injury, barrenness, and cold. This contrast clarifies how much the speaker believes dreams contribute to life.

## Historical context

The poem is commonly dated to 1922. A digital anthology records a related 1923 publication in The World Tomorrow, while other references identify 1922 as the poem’s date; this page uses 1922 as the catalog’s publication year.

Hughes was an important writer of the Harlem Renaissance. Read in that context, the poem’s insistence on preserving dreams can apply both to individual aspiration and to the threatened hopes of Black Americans living under segregation and racism.

## What critics say

> ““Dreams” revolves around two major metaphors. The speaker compares life after the loss of dreams to “a broken-winged bird / That cannot fly” and “a barren field / Frozen with snow.””
>
> — LitCharts, [Dreams Poem Summary and Analysis](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/langston-hughes/dreams)

> “The poem emphasizes the importance of holding onto dreams, especially during times of challenge.”
>
> — Rhode Island Foundation, [“Hold fast to dreams”](https://rifoundation.org/stories/hold-fast-to-dreams)

## Common questions

### What is the meaning of Langston Hughes’s “Dreams”?

The poem argues that dreams—especially hopes and aspirations—are necessary for a life with purpose, movement, and the possibility of growth.

### What are the main themes in “Dreams”?

Its main themes are hope, aspiration, loss, freedom, and the emotional barrenness that follows when people abandon their dreams.

### What literary devices does Hughes use in “Dreams”?

Hughes uses repetition, parallel structure, and two central metaphors: life without dreams becomes a broken-winged bird and a barren field frozen with snow.

### What is the form and meter of “Dreams”?

The poem has two quatrains and is closest to iambic dimeter, with short, varied lines and no fixed end-rhyme scheme.

## References

- [Dreams](https://poets.org/poem/dreams) — Academy of American Poets

- [Langston Hughes, “Dreams” (1923)](https://scalar.lehigh.edu/african-american-poetry-a-digital-anthology/langston-hughes-dreams-1923) — African-American Poetry: A Digital Anthology

- [Dreams Poem Summary and Analysis](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/langston-hughes/dreams) — LitCharts

# Each and All analysis

Each and All — Ralph Waldo Emerson (1839)

This Each and All analysis explains how Ralph Waldo Emerson turns a bird, seashells, and a lover’s bride into a meditation on beauty, perception, and the perfect whole.

## The poem

```
Little thinks, in the field, yon red-cloaked clown,
Of thee from the hill-top looking down;
The heifer that lows in the upland farm,
Far-heard, lows not thine ear to charm;
The sexton, tolling his bell at noon,
Deems not that great Napoleon
Stops his horse, and lists with delight,
Whilst his files sweep round yon Alpine height;
Nor knowest thou what argument
Thy life to thy neighbor’s creed has lent.
All are needed by each one;
Nothing is fair or good alone.
I thought the sparrow’s note from heaven,
Singing at dawn on the alder bough;
I brought him home, in his nest, at even;
He sings the song, but it pleases not now,
For I did not bring home the river and sky;
He sang to my ear,—they sang to my eye.
The delicate shells lay on the shore;
The bubbles of the latest wave
Fresh pearls to their enamel gave;
And the bellowing of the savage sea
Greeted their safe escape to me.
I wiped away the weeds and foam,
I fetched my sea-born treasures home;
But the poor, unsightly, noisome things
Had left their beauty on the shore,
With the sun, and the sand, and the wild uproar.
The lover watched his graceful maid,
As ’mid the virgin train she stayed,
Nor knew her beauty’s best attire
Was woven still by the snow-white choir.
At last she came to his hermitage,
Like the bird from the woodlands to the cage;—
The gay enchantment was undone,
A gentle wife, but fairy none.
Then I said, ‘I covet truth;
Beauty is unripe childhood’s cheat;
I leave it behind with the games of youth:’—
As I spoke, beneath my feet
The ground-pine curled its pretty wreath,
Running over the club-moss burrs;
I inhaled the violet’s breath;
Around me stood the oaks and firs;
Pine-cones and acorns lay on the ground;
Over me soared the eternal sky,
Full of light and of deity;
Again I saw, again I heard,
The rolling river, the morning bird;—
Beauty through my senses stole;
I yielded myself to the perfect whole.
```

Text from [Each and All by Ralph Waldo Emerson](https://poets.org/poem/each-and-all). Public domain in the US (First published in 1839, Each and All is in the public domain in the United States; the Academy of American Poets marks the poem as public domain.).

## Summary

The speaker begins with a series of scenes in which people, animals, and events affect one another without fully knowing it. The conclusion of that opening claim is that nothing is fair or good alone.

Three examples then test the idea: a sparrow loses its meaning indoors, shells lose their beauty away from the shore, and a woman’s enchantment disappears when the lover brings her into his hermitage. When the speaker finally returns to the whole natural scene, beauty comes back through all the senses.

## Meaning and interpretation

The poem’s central meaning is that beauty is relational rather than portable. The sparrow still sings and the shells remain physically present, but the river, sky, sun, sand, and sea that made them beautiful cannot be carried home with them.

The final movement complicates the speaker’s attempt to reject beauty in favor of truth. As PoetryVerse observes, the ending is not simply a choice of “beauty” over “truth”; it presents truth as inseparable from the whole sensory world. Yielding, rather than possessing, becomes the speaker’s way of understanding.

## Themes

### Organic unity

The refrain-like claim “All are needed by each one” makes each image part of a larger system. A person’s life, a bird’s song, and a landscape acquire significance through relationships that exceed the individual object.

### Beauty and context

The poem repeatedly removes something admired from its setting and records the loss. Beauty is shown as an event involving sound, light, place, motion, and memory, not as a permanent possession stored inside a thing.

### Possession versus participation

The speaker’s instinct is to bring the bird and shells home and to draw the beloved into a private hermitage. Each act of possession isolates what was admired. The ending reverses that movement when the speaker yields to the surrounding world.

### Limits of individual perspective

The opening images show that people are often unaware of the meanings their actions have for others. Emerson’s wider point is social as well as natural: each life contributes to a pattern that no single observer can completely see.

## Form and meter

Each and All is a 51-line poem presented as one continuous block rather than as separately titled stanzas. The poem’s argument unfolds through linked examples, so the uninterrupted shape reinforces its movement from parts toward a whole.

The dominant rhyme pattern is paired end rhyme, beginning with “clown”/“down” and “farm”/“charm.” Emerson varies the pattern with occasional half-rhyme, including “one”/“alone,” while internal pauses keep the long sentences conversational.

The lines use a flexible, songlike accentual rhythm rather than a single meter maintained without variation. Because the poem shifts between short statements, narrative lines, and descriptive lists, the open editor settings are more useful than forcing it into a fixed meter.

## Literary devices

### Refrain-like aphorism

> All are needed by each one; / Nothing is fair or good alone.

These compact lines state the poem’s governing principle after the opening examples. Their balanced syntax makes a philosophical claim sound memorable and almost proverbial.

### Sensory imagery

> The bubbles of the latest wave / Fresh pearls to their enamel gave;

Visual, auditory, and tactile details make the shore an active environment. When the shells are removed, the poem shows that their beauty included the sea’s motion and sound, not only their surfaces.

### Simile

> Like the bird from the woodlands to the cage;—

The comparison links the lover’s domestic ideal to the earlier act of caging the sparrow. It gives the poem’s romantic example an ethical tension: intimacy can become another form of removal.

### Anaphora and accumulation

> Again I saw, again I heard, / The rolling river, the morning bird;—

Repeated openings such as “The,” “I,” and “Again” gather separate details into a dense final perception. The accumulating list enacts the speaker’s renewed awareness of interdependence.

## Historical context

Each and All was first published in the Western Messenger on February 6, 1839, after being composed in the 1830s. Its public-domain status is confirmed by the Academy of American Poets.

Emerson was an American essayist, philosopher, and poet associated with Transcendentalism. The poem’s emphasis on nature, intuition, and the relation between individual parts and a larger unity aligns with concerns that also appear in his prose.

The poem’s language combines moral reflection with ordinary New England scenes and a striking reference to Napoleon in the Alps. That scale shift—from a field and farm to European history—helps establish the idea that local actions can participate in meanings their actors never intend.

## What critics say

> “Emerson depicts everything from birds to trees to the sky and the sea as connected to one another.”
>
> — Emma Baldwin; reviewed by the Poem Analysis Editorial Team, [Poem Analysis](https://poemanalysis.com/ralph-waldo-emerson/each-and-all/)

> “Beauty is shown to be not a coating on the object but a relationship among object, setting, and the forces that frame it.”
>
> — [PoetryVerse](https://www.poetryverse.com/ralph-waldo-emerson-poems/each-and-all/poem-analysis)

> “The poem is a good illustration of the notion of oversoul, the belief in organic metaphor.”
>
> — B. M. Karadağ, [Türk Dilbilim](https://turkdilbilim.wordpress.com/2020/10/11/each-and-all-by-emerson-an-analysis/)

## Common questions

### What is the main meaning of “Each and All”?

The poem argues that beauty and meaning depend on relationships. A bird, shell, or person loses something when separated from the landscape, community, and sensory conditions that give it significance.

### What are the main themes in “Each and All”?

Its main themes are organic unity, beauty in context, the limits of individual perception, and the danger of treating nature or other people as possessions.

### What is the form and meter of “Each and All”?

It is a 51-line block-form poem with paired end rhymes and a flexible, songlike rhythm. Its varied line lengths and changing syntax make it better understood as irregular accentual verse than as one fixed meter.

### Why does the speaker bring the sparrow and shells home?

He tries to possess and preserve things whose beauty impressed him in nature. Once removed from the river, sky, shore, sun, sand, and sea, they remain materially present but no longer produce the same experience.

## References

- [Full poem text and public-domain notice](https://poets.org/poem/each-and-all) — Academy of American Poets

- [Form, themes, and literary-device analysis](https://poemanalysis.com/ralph-waldo-emerson/each-and-all/) — Poem Analysis

- [Close reading of context, possession, and the perfect whole](https://www.poetryverse.com/ralph-waldo-emerson-poems/each-and-all/poem-analysis) — PoetryVerse

- [Organic unity and Emerson’s oversoul](https://turkdilbilim.wordpress.com/2020/10/11/each-and-all-by-emerson-an-analysis/) — Türk Dilbilim

# Fire and Ice analysis

Fire and Ice — Robert Frost (1920)

This Fire and Ice analysis explains how Robert Frost turns an end-of-the-world question into a study of desire, hatred, understatement, and poetic form.

## The poem

```
Some say the world will end in fire,
Some say in ice.
From what I’ve tasted of desire
I hold with those who favor fire.
But if it had to perish twice,
I think I know enough of hate
To say that for destruction ice
Is also great
And would suffice.
```

Text from [Fire and Ice](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/44263/fire-and-ice). Public domain in the US (First printed in Harper's Magazine in December 1920, so the poem is in the US public domain.).

## Summary

The speaker considers two predictions about how the world might end: fire or ice. Personal experience leads the speaker to favor fire, which is linked to desire.

The speaker then grants that ice would also be enough to destroy the world, because the speaker knows the power of hate. The poem ends by making both emotions adequate causes of catastrophe.

## Meaning and interpretation

Fire and ice work as elemental images for human emotions. Fire suggests desire that consumes and expands; ice suggests hatred or emotional coldness that hardens and separates.

The poem’s casual, almost conversational voice makes its subject more unsettling. The speaker discusses annihilation as though comparing two plausible options, and the modest word “suffice” reduces the end of the world to a question of adequacy.

The poem does not offer a reassuring third possibility. Its two alternatives differ in temperature and texture, but both reveal humanity’s capacity to turn feeling into destruction.

## Themes

### Desire and excess

The speaker’s phrase “tasted of desire” makes passion bodily and experiential. Fire represents desire when appetite grows hot enough to consume what surrounds it.

### Hatred and emotional coldness

Ice gives hate a physical form. Unlike spectacular fire, coldness can destroy through distance, indifference, fixation, and the slow hardening of relationships.

### Human self-destruction

The poem shifts from cosmic speculation to moral responsibility. The world-ending forces are not only astronomical elements; they are patterns of human feeling that can scale into collective ruin.

## Form and meter

“Fire and Ice” is a single nine-line stanza. Most lines are iambic tetrameter, while lines 2, 8, and 9 contract to iambic dimeter. The changing line lengths keep the poem close to speech while giving its ending a clipped finality.

The end-rhyme pattern is commonly represented as ABA ABC BCB: fire/desire, ice/twice/suffice, and hate/great interlock rather than resolving into separate blocks. The pattern has been read as a modified terza rima, a possible formal echo of Dante.

The poem’s nine lines and its narrowing close can suggest a descent or compression, but the Dante connection is an interpretive possibility rather than something the poem explains directly. lyriic’s editor setting foregrounds the dominant iambic tetrameter while the analysis notes the dimeter exceptions.

## Literary devices

### Extended metaphor

> Some say the world will end in fire, / Some say in ice.

The physical elements become figures for desire and hate. Frost keeps the metaphor compact, allowing the reader to move between planetary destruction and ordinary human emotion without a transition.

### Antithesis

> Some say ... fire, / Some say in ice.

The repeated opening phrase sets fire against ice and gives the poem a balanced debate. The apparent opposition eventually becomes an equivalence: either force would be enough.

### Understatement and irony

> Is also great / And would suffice.

“Suffice” usually means be enough, an unassuming word for global destruction. Its calm practicality clashes with the scale of the claim and creates the poem’s sharpest irony.

### Enjambment

> I think I know enough of hate / To say that for destruction ice

The sentence crosses the line break as the speaker measures personal knowledge of hate. The delayed conclusion makes the judgment feel deliberate rather than explosive.

## Historical context

The poem was first printed in Harper’s Magazine in December 1920 and later collected in New Hampshire: A Poem with Notes and Grace Notes in 1923. Its publication followed the First World War, a period when large-scale human destruction had become a newly immediate historical reality.

A later account by astronomer Harlow Shapley connected Frost’s poem with a conversation about whether the sun might destroy or freeze the Earth. That story is part of the poem’s publication lore, but the finished poem turns the scientific alternatives into a metaphor for human desire and hate.

Readers often connect the nine-line structure and modified terza-rima pattern with Dante’s Inferno. The connection is suggestive, especially because Dante’s Hell includes both fire and a frozen final circle, but it should be treated as an interpretive lens rather than a settled explanation of every detail.

## What critics say

> “The consistent iambs coupled with the varying line length create a breezy, conversational tone.”
>
> — LitCharts editors, [LitCharts](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/robert-frost/fire-and-ice)

> “The effect is structural irony: fire gets more verbal space, but ice gets the last word.”
>
> — Poetry Lovers’ Page editors, [Poetry Lovers’ Page](https://www.poetryloverspage.com/poets/frost/fire_and_ice/literary-analysis)

## Common questions

### What is the main meaning of “Fire and Ice”?

Frost presents desire and hate as two different but equally sufficient ways to destroy the world. The poem’s cosmic question becomes a warning about destructive human emotion.

### What do fire and ice symbolize?

Fire symbolizes consuming desire, passion, or appetite. Ice symbolizes hate, coldness, indifference, or emotional hardening. The poem does not make either force harmless.

### What is the rhyme scheme of “Fire and Ice”?

The rhyme scheme is commonly given as ABA ABC BCB. It interweaves the fire, ice, and hate rhyme families and is sometimes described as a modified terza rima.

### What is the meter of “Fire and Ice”?

Most lines are iambic tetrameter, but lines 2, 8, and 9 are shorter iambic dimeter lines. The variation supports the poem’s conversational sound and compressed ending.

## References

- [Poem text and first publication credit](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/44263/fire-and-ice) — Poetry Foundation

- [Poem text and December 1920 publication note](https://poets.org/poem/fire-and-ice) — Academy of American Poets

- [Form, meter, rhyme, and interpretation](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/robert-frost/fire-and-ice) — LitCharts

- [Literary analysis of form and imagery](https://www.poetryloverspage.com/poets/frost/fire_and_ice/literary-analysis) — Poetry Lovers’ Page

# First Fig analysis

First Fig — Edna St. Vincent Millay (1920)

This First Fig analysis explains how Edna St. Vincent Millay uses a double-burning candle, common meter, and defiant address to frame an intense life as brief but beautiful.

## The poem

```
My candle burns at both ends;
It will not last the night;
But ah, my foes, and oh, my friends—
It gives a lovely light!
```

Text from [First Fig by Edna St. Vincent Millay](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poetrymagazine/poems/14095/first-fig). Public domain in the US (The poem first appeared in Poetry in 1918 and was published in A Few Figs from Thistles in 1920; the Academy of American Poets identifies it as public domain.).

## Summary

The speaker compares their life to a candle burning at both ends. That choice promises a shorter duration, but it produces an especially vivid light.

In four compact lines, the speaker accepts both admiration and opposition. Friends and foes are invited to watch the flame, while the speaker refuses to apologize for its intensity.

## Meaning and interpretation

The candle is an extended metaphor for a life spent with unusual energy, appetite, or creative and erotic freedom. The poem does not specify one behavior, so the image remains open to several forms of wholehearted living.

The final exclamation changes the apparent warning about exhaustion into a celebration. Millay’s speaker values the quality and brightness of experience even while acknowledging that it cannot last.

## Themes

### Intensity and transience

A candle burning at both ends consumes itself quickly, making brilliance inseparable from limitation. The poem treats a short, vivid life as a meaningful alternative to a longer but more restrained one.

### Independence and defiance

By addressing “my foes” and “my friends” together, the speaker places public judgment beneath personal choice. Approval and disapproval matter less than the speaker’s decision to live fully.

### Beauty in the present

The last line concentrates attention on what the flame gives now: “a lovely light.” The poem’s perspective favors immediate experience over promises about the future.

## Form and meter

“First Fig” is a single quatrain with the compact, alternating movement of common meter: long and short lines built from iambic tetrameter and trimeter. The poem is also a ballad-stanza variation rather than a perfectly regular exercise.

The end rhymes form an ABAB pattern: “ends”/“friends” and “night”/“light.” The neat rhyme and quick rhythm make the speaker’s declaration memorable and almost songlike.

The opening line bends the expected rhythm with seven syllables and the forceful stresses of “both ends.” That compression makes the line sound abruptly cut short, echoing the life the speaker says will not last the night.

## Literary devices

### Extended metaphor

> My candle burns at both ends;

The candle stands for the speaker’s life or way of living. Burning it at both ends joins brilliance to self-consumption, so the image carries both pleasure and risk.

### Apostrophe

> But ah, my foes, and oh, my friends—

The speaker turns outward to address absent or generalized listeners. Naming enemies and friends together makes the declaration public and emphasizes that neither group controls the speaker’s choices.

### Alliteration and sound pattern

> My candle burns at both ends

The repeated b sound gives the opening force and momentum. In the last line, the softer pairing of “lovely light” makes the flame sound attractive as well as dangerous.

### Caesura and punctuation

> But ah, my foes, and oh, my friends—

The semicolon, comma, and dash create pauses that shape the speaker’s performance. The pauses slow the address just before the emphatic, exclamatory conclusion.

## Historical context

“First Fig” appeared in Poetry in 1918 and became the opening poem of A Few Figs from Thistles, published in book form in 1920. The poem therefore belongs to Millay’s early public career and to the cultural changes associated with the start of the 1920s.

The collection’s frank treatment of unconventional women’s lives and sexuality helped make Millay a prominent Greenwich Village literary figure. The poem’s speaker can be read in that context, but the text itself leaves the candle’s exact meaning deliberately unspecified.

The poem’s familiar candle image also gives its modern subject a traditional lyric frame. Its regular rhyme and meter make the speaker’s rebellious claim sound polished, witty, and easy to remember.

## What critics say

> “The speaker ... celebrates going your own way and taking life by the horns.”
>
> — [LitCharts](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/edna-st-vincent-millay/first-fig)

> “The poems in this short series debunk a conservative economy of time and work to celebrate counter-cultural women's values and outlooks that have been traditionally coded as male terrain.”
>
> — [Textual Cultures](https://scholarworks.iu.edu/journals/index.php/textual/article/download/2117/26571/45516)

## Common questions

### What is the main meaning of “First Fig”?

The poem celebrates living intensely and independently even when that life may be brief or exhausting. Its speaker values a bright present over a safer, more restrained existence.

### What does the candle symbolize in “First Fig”?

The candle symbolizes the speaker’s life and possibly creative, social, or erotic energy. Burning at both ends suggests using that energy quickly and fully.

### What is the form and meter of “First Fig”?

It is a four-line quatrain using a common-meter or ballad-stanza pattern, with alternating iambic tetrameter and trimeter and an ABAB rhyme scheme. The first line includes a deliberate rhythmic compression.

### Why does the speaker mention both foes and friends?

The paired address shows that the speaker expects mixed reactions but refuses to let either praise or criticism determine how they live. Both groups are asked to witness the same bright, temporary flame.

## References

- [Poem text and 1918 publication credit](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poetrymagazine/poems/14095/first-fig) — The Poetry Foundation

- [Poem text and public-domain notice](https://poets.org/index%2Ephp/poem/first-fig) — Academy of American Poets

- [Form, meter, themes, and context](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/edna-st-vincent-millay/first-fig) — LitCharts

- [Scholarly history of A Few Figs from Thistles](https://scholarworks.iu.edu/journals/index.php/textual/article/download/2117/26571/45516) — Textual Cultures

## Open the editor

# Fog analysis

Fog — Carl Sandburg (1916)

This Fog analysis explains how Carl Sandburg uses an extended cat metaphor, compressed free verse, and a harbor-city setting to make a brief arrival and departure feel mysterious.

## The poem

```
The fog comes
on little cat feet.

It sits looking
over harbor and city
on silent haunches
and then moves on.
```

Text from [Fog by Carl Sandburg](https://poets.org/poem/fog). Public domain in the US (The Academy of American Poets identifies this poem as public domain; it first appeared in Chicago Poems in 1916.).

## Summary

The speaker presents fog as a creature that arrives quietly, settles over a harbor and city, watches for a moment, and then leaves.

The poem’s central image compares fog to a cat. Its small feet, silent haunches, and independent movement give an ordinary weather event the presence of a living observer.

## Meaning and interpretation

Sandburg makes the fog feel active without explaining or personifying it through a long narrative. The cat metaphor lets readers sense its stealth, patience, and self-possession.

The final phrase, “and then moves on,” keeps the poem open-ended. The fog does not conquer or transform the city; it visits, changes perception briefly, and disappears.

## Themes

### The mystery of nature

The fog is familiar but difficult to understand. By giving it catlike behavior, Sandburg makes the natural world seem alert, independent, and slightly unknowable.

### Transience

The poem follows a complete arc from arrival to departure in six short lines. Its brevity mirrors fog’s temporary presence and the fleeting nature of observation.

### Nature and the city

The fog moves over both “harbor and city,” placing a soft, shapeless natural force above an organized urban landscape. The city becomes a scene the fog can quietly inspect.

## Form and meter

“Fog” is a six-line free-verse poem arranged as a two-line couplet followed by a four-line stanza. The first stanza introduces the cat metaphor; the second shows the fog sitting, looking, and moving away.

There is no fixed meter or rhyme scheme. The varied line lengths and plain syntax create a flexible, quiet rhythm that suits the fog’s unannounced movement.

The poem’s three-part progression—coming, sitting and looking, then moving on—gives the miniature a complete shape. Its compression and focus on one concrete natural image also recall haiku, though it is not a traditional Japanese haiku.

## Literary devices

### Extended metaphor

> The fog comes / on little cat feet

The poem sustains the comparison between fog and cat through “feet,” “sits,” “haunches,” and “moves on.” The metaphor makes the fog seem alive and self-directed.

### Personification

> It sits looking / over harbor and city

Fog is given the posture and attention of an animal watching a scene. This turns passive weather into a quiet presence with apparent agency.

### Alliteration and consonance

> little cat feet

The repeated l, c, and t sounds make the opening image tactile and lightly percussive. The sound pattern suggests the delicate approach of the imagined cat.

### Enjambment

> It sits looking / over harbor and city

The line break delays the object of “looking,” extending the fog’s gaze across the page and allowing the city to emerge gradually.

## Historical context

“Fog” first appeared in Sandburg’s 1916 collection Chicago Poems. Sandburg was living and working in Chicago, a city whose harbor and rapid industrial growth often shaped his poetry.

The poem is commonly associated with Sandburg’s attempt to make an American version of haiku: a brief, free, image-centered poem rather than a strict imitation of Japanese form.

Chicago is a plausible setting because the poem names a harbor and appeared in Chicago Poems, but the text never identifies the city. Its deliberately spare setting allows the fog to belong to any harbor city.

## What critics say

> “The comparison makes the fog, which readers might take for an ordinary natural phenomenon, seem mysterious and unknowable.”
>
> — [LitCharts](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/carl-sandburg/fog)

> “The loveliness of ... a fog coming on “little cat feet,”—the incommunicable loveliness of the earth, of life—is too keen to be borne.”
>
> — Harriet Monroe, [Harriet Monroe, quoted in Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fog_(poem))

## Common questions

### What is the main meaning of “Fog”?

The poem presents fog as a quiet, catlike visitor. Its brief appearance suggests the mystery and beauty of nature, as well as the transience of any single moment.

### Why does Sandburg compare fog to a cat?

Cats can move silently, appear and disappear quickly, and watch from a still position. Those qualities help Sandburg make the fog feel alive, independent, and slightly mysterious.

### What poetic form does “Fog” use?

“Fog” is free verse: it has six lines, two stanzas, no fixed meter, and no regular rhyme scheme. Its compact, image-driven structure resembles Sandburg’s idea of an American haiku.

### Is “Fog” about Chicago?

Chicago is a likely context because Sandburg lived there and the poem appeared in Chicago Poems, but the poem only says “harbor and city.” Its setting remains intentionally open.

## References

- [Poem text and public-domain notice](https://poets.org/poem/fog) — Academy of American Poets

- [Chicago Poems text and bibliographic record](https://www.bartleby.com/lit-hub/chicago-poems/56-fog) — Bartleby

- [Publication history and reception](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fog_(poem)) — Wikipedia

- [Form, devices, and context](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/carl-sandburg/fog) — LitCharts

# Go and Catch a Falling Star analysis

Song: Go and catch a falling star — John Donne (1633)

This Go and Catch a Falling Star analysis explains how John Donne turns magical impossibilities and a playful song form into a bitter argument about fidelity.

## The poem

```
GO and catch a falling star,
Get with child a mandrake root,
Tell me where all past years are,
Or who cleft the Devil's foot:
Teach me to hear mermaids singing,
Or to keep off envy's stinging,
And find
What wind
Serves to advance an honest mind.

If thou be'st born to strange sights,
Things invisible to see,
Ride ten thousand days and nights
Till Age snow white hairs on thee;
Thou, when thou return'st, wilt tell me
All strange wonders that befell thee,
And swear
No where
Lives a woman true and fair.

If thou find'st one, let me know;
Such a pilgrimage were sweet.
Yet do not; I would not go,
Though at next door we might meet.
Though she were true when you met her,
And last till you write your letter,
Yet she
Will be
False, ere I come, to two or three.
```

Text from [Song — full poem](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Song:_Go_and_catch_a_falling_star). Public domain in the US (First published in the 1633 edition of Donne's collected poems, well before the US public-domain cutoff.).

## Summary

The speaker commands a listener to perform a series of impossible or supernatural tasks, including catching a falling star, finding lost time, and hearing mermaids sing.

The listener is then asked to travel for ten thousand days in search of a woman who is both true and fair. The final stanza reverses its apparent invitation: even if such a woman were found, the speaker says her fidelity would fail before he could reach her.

## Meaning and interpretation

The poem makes romantic fidelity seem less attainable than its opening marvels. Donne's speaker uses hyperbole and a fantastical quest to turn a conventional complaint about infidelity into a witty, memorable paradox: magical sights may be discoverable, but a faithful and beautiful woman is not.

The confident conclusion is also a performance by a speaker whose cynicism may be covering disappointment. The poem invites criticism of its misogynistic generalization while showing how smoothly a song, rhyme, and comic escalation can make that generalization sound persuasive.

## Themes

### Fidelity and skepticism

The repeated search for a woman who is both true and fair becomes an impossible quest. The poem's final claim that faithfulness would end almost immediately turns skepticism into a totalizing judgment.

### Gender and power

The speaker treats women's supposed infidelity as a universal fact rather than an individual possibility. That generalization reflects a misogynistic literary convention, and its force depends on the speaker controlling the terms of the argument.

### Wonder and disillusionment

Stars, mandrakes, mermaids, the devil, and a ten-thousand-day journey create a world of marvels. The poem then uses that imaginative world to make its conclusion more disillusioned: even wonders cannot produce the lover the speaker wants.

## Form and meter

The poem has three nine-line stanzas. Each stanza follows the same ABABCCDDD rhyme scheme, giving the argument a brisk, song-like momentum.

The predominant rhythm is trochaic tetrameter: many lines move through four stressed-unstressed beats, as in “GO and catch a falling star.” Lines seven and eight contract to short iambic monometers—“And find / What wind”—which sharply emphasize the speaker's punchlines.

The regular musical form creates tension with the speaker's harsh conclusion. The poem sounds light and controlled even as its argument becomes increasingly absolute.

## Literary devices

### Hyperbole

> Ride ten thousand days and nights

The enormous journey makes the search for a faithful woman sound beyond ordinary human effort. Exaggeration lets the speaker compare romantic fidelity with supernatural impossibilities.

### Apostrophe and imperative

> Go and catch a falling star

The opening command addresses an unnamed listener directly. Its energetic imperatives make the poem feel like spoken banter while launching the speaker's impossible test.

### Allusion and folklore

> Get with child a mandrake root

The mandrake, mermaids, and the devil's cleft foot draw on supernatural and folkloric imagery. These references build a catalogue of strange possibilities against which human constancy is judged.

### Irony

> Such a pilgrimage were sweet. / Yet do not; I would not go

The speaker first welcomes news of a faithful woman, then immediately refuses the journey. This reversal exposes the gap between his stated desire and his settled expectation of disappointment.

## Historical context

The poem was first published posthumously in 1633, two years after Donne's death, in the first collected edition of his poems. It circulated in manuscript before that publication, as was common for poems shared within literary circles.

The poem belongs to the early modern tradition of witty complaints about women's inconstancy. Its speaker's claim is not a neutral description of relationships: it is a gendered literary posture that contemporary readers can examine as both clever rhetoric and prejudice.

## What critics say

> “The poem's rhyme scheme, relatively steady meter, and clear hyperbole make its tone feel light-hearted and satirical, but the speaker also seems to harbor genuine melancholy, bitterness, and cynicism towards women and relationships.”
>
> — [LitCharts](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/john-donne/song-go-and-catch-a-falling-star)

> “The analysis reveals anti-feministic undertones within the broader context, where societal norms and power dynamics played a crucial role in shaping discourse.”
>
> — Malik Umer Ajmal and Tayyaba Zainab, [Journal of Applied Linguistics](https://journal.eltaorganization.org/index.php/joal/article/view/177)

## Common questions

### What is the main meaning of “Go and Catch a Falling Star”?

The speaker argues that finding a woman who is both beautiful and faithful is as impossible as completing a supernatural quest. The poem presents that claim as witty, but its cynicism also reveals bitterness and a misogynistic assumption.

### What are the main themes in the poem?

The main themes are fidelity, skepticism, gender, wonder, and disillusionment. Donne contrasts magical discoveries with the speaker's belief that romantic constancy cannot last.

### What form and meter does the poem use?

It has three nine-line stanzas with an ABABCCDDD rhyme scheme. Most lines use forceful trochaic tetrameter, while the short seventh and eighth lines of each stanza work as emphatic iambic monometers.

### Why does Donne use impossible tasks?

The impossible tasks create a scale for the speaker's claim: catching a star, finding lost time, or hearing mermaids may be imaginable, but locating a permanently faithful woman is presented as even less likely.

## References

- [Song — full poem](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Song:_Go_and_catch_a_falling_star) — Wikisource

- [Song: Go and catch a falling star — summary and analysis](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/john-donne/song-go-and-catch-a-falling-star) — LitCharts

- [Critical discourse analysis of the poem](https://journal.eltaorganization.org/index.php/joal/article/view/177) — Journal of Applied Linguistics

# Goblin Feet analysis

Goblin Feet — J. R. R. Tolkien (1915)

Read J. R. R. Tolkien’s Goblin Feet as a spell-like journey into a small, vivid fairy world. This analysis explains the poem’s meaning, imagery, sound, form, and final turn from wonder to loss.

## The poem

```
I am off down the road
Where the fairy lanterns glowed
And the little pretty flitter-mice are flying:
A slender band of grey
It runs creepily away
And the hedges and the grasses are a-sighing.
The air is full of wings,
And of blundery beetle-things
That warn you with their whirring and their humming.
O! I hear the tiny horns
Of enchanted leprechauns
And the padded feet of many gnomes a-coming!

O! the lights: O! the gleams:
O! the little twinkly sounds:
O! the rustle of their noiseless little robes:
O! the echo of their feet—of their happy little feet:
O! the swinging lamps in the starlit globes.

I must follow in their train
Down the crooked fairy lane
Where the coney-rabbits long ago have gone.
And where silvery they sing
In a moving moonlit ring
All a twinkle with the jewels they have on.
They are fading round the turn
Where the glow worms palely burn
And the echo of their padding feet is dying!
O! it’s knocking at my heart—
Let me go! O! let me start!
For the little magic hours are all a-flying.

O! the warmth! O! the hum!
O! the colours in the dark!
O! the gauzy wings of golden honey-flies!
O! the music of their feet—of their dancing goblin feet!
O! the magic! O! the sorrow when it dies.
```

Text from [Goblin Feet — Wikisource](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Goblin_Feet). Public domain in the US (First published in Oxford Poetry 1915, Goblin Feet is in the public domain in the United States because it was published before January 1, 1931.).

## Summary

The speaker follows a procession of tiny supernatural beings through a moonlit landscape. Fairy lanterns, flying creatures, glow-worms, jewels, and padded feet turn an ordinary road into a hidden world that seems to invite participation.

The poem’s delight is inseparable from its disappearance. The procession fades around a turn, and the speaker’s urgent wish to follow ends with the recognition that magic brings sorrow when it dies.

## Meaning and interpretation

Goblin Feet presents enchantment as an experience of sensory abundance: the speaker hears humming, horns, rustling robes, and rhythmic feet while seeing lamps, colours, jewels, and wings. The repeated exclamations make wonder feel immediate and almost breathless.

The poem also understands wonder as temporary. The speaker is drawn after the fairies, but the central movement is away from the speaker: their echo dies, the magic hours fly, and the final line names the grief produced by their passing. The meaning is therefore not simply that fairy life is beautiful; it is that beauty becomes poignant because it cannot be held.

## Themes

### Wonder and enchantment

The poem builds a complete fairy atmosphere from light, sound, movement, and diminutive beings. Its catalog of sensations makes the supernatural world feel close enough to enter.

### Transience and loss

The fairies fade, their footsteps become an echo, and the speaker’s excitement turns to sorrow. The poem treats enchantment as something whose departure is part of its emotional power.

### Desire to cross into another world

The repeated wish to follow, go, and start turns observation into pursuit. The speaker is not satisfied with seeing the fairy procession; they want to leave the ordinary road behind and join it.

## Form and meter

The poem has four stanzas, alternating a twelve-line descriptive stanza with a six-line exclamatory stanza. Its lines use a flexible accentual-syllabic rhythm rather than one fixed meter, so the poem feels closer to a song or incantation than to a strict metrical exercise.

End rhyme and internal sound patterning help hold the irregular lines together: “flying” answers “a-sighing,” while “humming” answers “a-coming.” The short exclamatory lines in the second and fourth stanzas create choruses, and the repeated “O!” gives the poem a breathless, performative pulse.

Because the rhythm changes with the speaker’s excitement, an open editor setting is more useful than imposing a single meter. Counts can still help readers notice how Tolkien varies line length for speed, emphasis, and musical effect.

## Literary devices

### Alliteration and onomatopoeia

> “their whirring and their humming”

The repeated consonants and sound-imitating words make the invisible fairy traffic audible. The poem asks readers to hear the world before they can fully see it.

### Sensory imagery

> “O! the colours in the dark!”

Visual, auditory, and tactile details accumulate across the poem. The fairies are defined less by explanation than by the sensations surrounding their movement.

### Repetition and refrain-like exclamation

> “O! the echo of their feet—of their happy little feet”

Repeated words such as “little,” “feet,” and “O!” establish a childlike, incantatory voice. The repetitions also make the final “sorrow” feel like a deliberate reversal of the earlier delight.

### Personification

> “the hedges and the grasses are a-sighing”

The landscape participates in the fairy world. Plants, insects, lamps, and echoes all seem animated, so the road becomes a responsive threshold rather than a passive setting.

## Historical context

Goblin Feet was written on April 27–28, 1915, and published in Oxford Poetry 1915 by B. H. Blackwell in December 1915. Tolkien Library identifies it as one of Tolkien’s early fairy poems and lists Tolkien among the volume’s contributors.

The Tolkien Library account says Tolkien wrote the poem to please Edith Bratt, who loved “spring and flowers and trees, and little elfin people.” It describes the poem as closely aligned with the Victorian depiction of fairies, which helps explain its small scale, bright enchantment, and emphasis on delicate movement.

The poem also records an early stage in Tolkien’s changing conception of fairies. Tolkien later disliked the work’s diminutive fairy tradition; a reported 1971 response called it “the unhappy little thing” he wished could be buried. That later reaction adds historical tension, but it does not erase the poem’s carefully sustained music and atmosphere.

## What critics say

> “The result was as close to the Victorian depiction of fairies as it can get.”
>
> — Tolkien Library, [Goblin Feet, a poem by J. R. R. Tolkien](https://tolkienlibrary.com/press/oxfordpoetry1915.php)

> “I wish the unhappy little thing, representing all that I came (so soon after) to fervently dislike, could be buried for ever”
>
> — Tolkien Library, [Goblin Feet, a poem by J. R. R. Tolkien](https://tolkienlibrary.com/press/oxfordpoetry1915.php)

## Common questions

### What is the meaning of Goblin Feet?

The poem presents enchantment as beautiful but temporary. The speaker longs to follow a fairy procession, then feels sorrow when its music, warmth, and footsteps fade.

### What are the main themes in Goblin Feet?

The main themes are wonder, fairy enchantment, sensory imagination, the desire to enter another world, and the sadness created by the passing of beauty.

### What form and meter does Goblin Feet use?

It has four alternating twelve-line and six-line stanzas. Its rhythm is flexible and songlike rather than strictly regular, with rhyme, alliteration, repetition, and exclamations creating its incantatory movement.

### Why did Tolkien later dislike Goblin Feet?

Tolkien later rejected the poem’s small, Victorian-style fairy imagery, which differed from the more substantial and mythic conception of elves he developed afterward. His later dislike is part of the poem’s history, not a substitute for reading its language.

## References

- [Goblin Feet — full text and public-domain notice](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Goblin_Feet) — Wikisource

- [Goblin Feet, a poem by J. R. R. Tolkien](https://tolkienlibrary.com/press/oxfordpoetry1915.php) — Tolkien Library

- [Oxford Poetry 1915 publication details](https://tolkienlibrary.com/booksedited/oxfordp/description.php) — Tolkien Library

## Open the editor

Write with this poem’s rhythm in the editor: https://lyriic.com/write
