# The Raven analysis

The Raven — Edgar Allan Poe (1845)

Read The Raven with a close look at its grief-stricken speaker, haunting refrain, and tightly controlled sound. This analysis explains the poem’s meaning, themes, form, and key devices.

## The poem

```
Once upon a midnight dreary, while I pondered, weak and weary,
Over many a quaint and curious volume of forgotten lore—
While I nodded, nearly napping, suddenly there came a tapping,
As of some one gently rapping, rapping at my chamber door.
“’Tis some visitor,” I muttered, “tapping at my chamber door—
Only this and nothing more.”

Ah, distinctly I remember it was in the bleak December;
And each separate dying ember wrought its ghost upon the floor.
Eagerly I wished the morrow;—vainly I had sought to borrow
From my books surcease of sorrow—sorrow for the lost Lenore—
For the rare and radiant maiden whom the angels name Lenore—
Nameless here for evermore.

And the silken, sad, uncertain rustling of each purple curtain
Thrilled me—filled me with fantastic terrors never felt before;
So that now, to still the beating of my heart, I stood repeating
“’Tis some visitor entreating entrance at my chamber door—
Some late visitor entreating entrance at my chamber door;—
This it is and nothing more.”

Presently my soul grew stronger; hesitating then no longer,
“Sir,” said I, “or Madam, truly your forgiveness I implore;
But the fact is I was napping, and so gently you came rapping,
And so faintly you came tapping, tapping at my chamber door,
That I scarce was sure I heard you”—here I opened wide the door;—
Darkness there and nothing more.

Deep into that darkness peering, long I stood there wondering, fearing,
Doubting, dreaming dreams no mortal ever dared to dream before;
But the silence was unbroken, and the stillness gave no token,
And the only word there spoken was the whispered word, “Lenore?”
This I whispered, and an echo murmured back the word, “Lenore!”—
Merely this and nothing more.

Back into the chamber turning, all my soul within me burning,
Soon again I heard a tapping somewhat louder than before.
“Surely,” said I, “surely that is something at my window lattice;
Let me see, then, what thereat is, and this mystery explore—
Let my heart be still a moment and this mystery explore;—
’Tis the wind and nothing more!”

Open here I flung the shutter, when, with many a flirt and flutter,
In there stepped a stately Raven of the saintly days of yore;
Not the least obeisance made he; not a minute stopped or stayed he;
But, with mien of lord or lady, perched above my chamber door—
Perched upon a bust of Pallas just above my chamber door—
Perched, and sat, and nothing more.

Then this ebony bird beguiling my sad fancy into smiling,
By the grave and stern decorum of the countenance it wore,
“Though thy crest be shorn and shaven, thou,” I said, “art sure no craven,
Ghastly grim and ancient Raven wandering from the Nightly shore—
Tell me what thy lordly name is on the Night’s Plutonian shore!”
Quoth the Raven “Nevermore.”

Much I marvelled this ungainly fowl to hear discourse so plainly,
Though its answer little meaning—little relevancy bore;
For we cannot help agreeing that no living human being
Ever yet was blessed with seeing bird above his chamber door—
Bird or beast upon the sculptured bust above his chamber door,
With such name as “Nevermore.”

But the Raven, sitting lonely on the placid bust, spoke only
That one word, as if his soul in that one word he did outpour.
Nothing farther then he uttered—not a feather then he fluttered—
Till I scarcely more than muttered “Other friends have flown before—
On the morrow he will leave me, as my Hopes have flown before.”
Then the bird said “Nevermore.”

Startled at the stillness broken by reply so aptly spoken,
“Doubtless,” said I, “what it utters is its only stock and store
Caught from some unhappy master whom unmerciful Disaster
Followed fast and followed faster till his songs one burden bore—
Till the dirges of his Hope that melancholy burden bore
Of ‘Never—nevermore’.”

But the Raven still beguiling all my fancy into smiling,
Straight I wheeled a cushioned seat in front of bird, and bust and door;
Then, upon the velvet sinking, I betook myself to linking
Fancy unto fancy, thinking what this ominous bird of yore—
What this grim, ungainly, ghastly, gaunt, and ominous bird of yore
Meant in croaking “Nevermore.”

This I sat engaged in guessing, but no syllable expressing
To the fowl whose fiery eyes now burned into my bosom’s core;
This and more I sat divining, with my head at ease reclining
On the cushion’s velvet lining that the lamp-light gloated o’er,
But whose velvet-violet lining with the lamp-light gloating o’er,
She shall press, ah, nevermore!

Then, methought, the air grew denser, perfumed from an unseen censer
Swung by Seraphim whose foot-falls tinkled on the tufted floor.
“Wretch,” I cried, “thy God hath lent thee—by these angels he hath sent thee
Respite—respite and nepenthe from thy memories of Lenore;
Quaff, oh quaff this kind nepenthe and forget this lost Lenore!”
Quoth the Raven “Nevermore.”

“Prophet!” said I, “thing of evil!—prophet still, if bird or devil!—
Whether Tempter sent, or whether tempest tossed thee here ashore,
Desolate yet all undaunted, on this desert land enchanted—
On this home by Horror haunted—tell me truly, I implore—
Is there—is there balm in Gilead?—tell me—tell me, I implore!”
Quoth the Raven “Nevermore.”

“Prophet!” said I, “thing of evil!—prophet still, if bird or devil!
By that Heaven that bends above us—by that God we both adore—
Tell this soul with sorrow laden if, within the distant Aidenn,
It shall clasp a sainted maiden whom the angels name Lenore—
Clasp a rare and radiant maiden whom the angels name Lenore.”
Quoth the Raven “Nevermore.”

“Be that word our sign of parting, bird or fiend!” I shrieked, upstarting—
“Get thee back into the tempest and the Night’s Plutonian shore!
Leave no black plume as a token of that lie thy soul hath spoken!
Leave my loneliness unbroken!—quit the bust above my door!
Take thy beak from out my heart, and take thy form from off my door!”
Quoth the Raven “Nevermore.”

And the Raven, never flitting, still is sitting, still is sitting
On the pallid bust of Pallas just above my chamber door;
And his eyes have all the seeming of a demon’s that is dreaming,
And the lamp-light o’er him streaming throws his shadow on the floor;
And my soul from out that shadow that lies floating on the floor
Shall be lifted—nevermore!
```

Text from [The Raven](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/48860/the-raven). Public domain in the US (First published in 1845, The Raven is in the public domain in the United States.).

## Summary

On a bleak December night, a grieving speaker hears tapping at his chamber door and window. A raven enters, perches above the door, and answers every question with one word: “Nevermore.”

The speaker gradually turns the bird’s repeated response into a verdict on his grief: he will not forget Lenore, find relief, or reunite with her after death. The final image leaves him trapped beneath the raven’s shadow.

## Meaning and interpretation

The poem presents grief as an interpretive loop. The raven may have learned “Nevermore” from a former master, but the speaker supplies the word’s increasingly painful meanings himself.

Lenore is both a lost beloved and the center of the speaker’s hope for spiritual reunion. By the end, “Nevermore” has become less a bird’s answer than the speaker’s conclusion that sorrow will outlast him.

## Themes

### Grief and memory

The speaker turns to books for “surcease of sorrow,” but memory of Lenore keeps returning. His repeated questions show mourning changing from remembrance into fixation.

### Loss of hope

“Nevermore” first sounds like a strange, possibly meaningless word. Each new question loads it with more finality until it denies earthly comfort and the hope of reunion in “Aidenn.”

### The supernatural and the psychological

The raven can be read as an ominous supernatural visitor, but the poem also makes the speaker’s mind central. The bird’s fixed answer becomes terrifying because the speaker interprets it through his own despair.

## Form and meter

The Raven is an eighteen-stanza narrative ballad. Each stanza has six lines and follows an ABCBBB end-rhyme pattern, with the final line sharply shortening the stanza.

The traditional meter is trochaic octameter: a falling rhythm built from eight trochaic feet. Poe varies the pattern through catalexis, pauses, and shortened lines, making “Nevermore” land like a final blow.

Internal rhyme, repeated end sounds in “-ore,” and the refrain create a dense, incantatory sound. The form’s regular return mirrors the speaker’s inability to move beyond grief.

## Literary devices

### Internal rhyme

> “Once upon a midnight dreary, while I pondered, weak and weary”

Rhyme inside the line adds musical pressure before the stanza’s end rhyme. It makes the speaker’s thoughts feel tightly linked and difficult to escape.

### Alliteration

> “While I nodded, nearly napping”

Repeated consonants make the language tactile and audible. In passages such as “weak and weary” and “silken, sad, uncertain,” sound helps build the poem’s hypnotic, uneasy mood.

### Refrain and repetition

> “Quoth the Raven ‘Nevermore.’”

The repeated word changes meaning according to the speaker’s question. Its recurrence turns a possible trick of language into an apparent prophecy of permanent loss.

### Allusion and symbolism

> “Perched upon a bust of Pallas”

The bust of Pallas Athena places the raven above a figure associated with wisdom, while “Plutonian shore,” “balm in Gilead,” and “Aidenn” connect the scene to death, healing, and the afterlife.

## Historical context

Poe’s poem was first published in 1845 by Wiley and Putnam in The Raven and Other Poems. Its public-domain status in the United States permits the full text here.

Poe’s 1846 essay “The Philosophy of Composition” discusses the poem’s intended unity of effect, melancholy tone, refrain, and formal construction. Readers and critics continue to debate how literally that account should be taken.

## What critics say

> ““The Raven” is a ballad utilizing trochaic octameter, which is not a common pattern in English language verse. It also follows the ABCBBB rhyme scheme, as highlighted, and additionally contains some internal rhyme, or rhyme within the same line.”
>
> — LeDavid Olmstead, [Tales of Edgar Allan Poe: Critical and Creative Editions](https://pressbooks.uiowa.edu/poetales/chapter/ledavid-olmstead-main-text/)

> “‘The Raven’ by Edgar Allan Poe is a ballad of eighteen six-line stanzas. Throughout, the poet uses trochaic octameter, a very distinctive metrical form.”
>
> — [Poem Analysis](https://poemanalysis.com/edgar-allan-poe/the-raven/)

## Common questions

### What is the meaning of The Raven?

The poem shows a grieving speaker turning a raven’s repeated “Nevermore” into a statement that his loss, loneliness, and lack of spiritual hope will never end.

### Who is Lenore in The Raven?

Lenore is the speaker’s deceased beloved. She is named as a “rare and radiant maiden,” and his questions about her make personal grief the poem’s emotional center.

### What does “Nevermore” mean in the poem?

At first it may be only a learned word, but the speaker gives it progressively darker meanings: no more visitors, no more relief from grief, and no reunion with Lenore.

### What meter does The Raven use?

The poem is traditionally described as trochaic octameter, with eight falling feet in its long lines. Its shortened closing lines, internal rhyme, and refrain create the characteristic pounding, musical effect.

## References

- [The Raven](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/48860/the-raven) — Poetry Foundation

- [The Raven: Critical and Creative Editions](https://pressbooks.uiowa.edu/poetales/chapter/ledavid-olmstead-main-text/) — University of Iowa Pressbooks

- [Understand The Raven by Edgar Allan Poe](https://poemanalysis.com/edgar-allan-poe/the-raven/) — Poem Analysis

## Open the editor

Write with this poem’s meter in the editor: https://lyriic.com/write

# The Red Wheelbarrow analysis

The Red Wheelbarrow — William Carlos Williams (1923)

This analysis explains how William Carlos Williams makes an ordinary farm tool newly visible through Imagist precision, color, and line breaks. Read the full poem, its meaning, form, themes, and key devices.

## The poem

```
so much depends
upon

a red wheel
barrow

glazed with rain
water

beside the white
chickens
```

Text from [The Red Wheelbarrow](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/45502/the-red-wheelbarrow). Public domain in the US (First published in the United States in 1923, the poem is in the US public domain.).

## Summary

The poem consists of one sentence: so much depends upon a red wheelbarrow glazed with rainwater beside white chickens. It offers no explanation for what depends on the object, leaving the reader inside a moment of attention.

Williams divides the sentence into four two-line stanzas. The wheelbarrow, the rainwater, and the chickens are ordinary concrete things, but the poem’s opening claim makes their presence feel necessary and consequential.

## Meaning and interpretation

The phrase “so much depends” creates productive uncertainty. It may point to the wheelbarrow’s practical value in farm work, but the poem never reduces the image to a single paraphrasable lesson. Its force comes from making us look closely at something we might otherwise overlook.

The poem enacts Williams’s idea of grounding ideas in things. Instead of naming an abstract feeling about labor, nature, or necessity, it gives us red paint, rainwater, and white chickens, allowing significance to emerge from perception.

The color contrast and wet surface make the scene vivid without turning it into an elaborate symbol. The wheelbarrow remains a useful object beside living animals, and the poem’s quiet claim is that ordinary material conditions can support an entire human world.

## Themes

### The importance of ordinary things

The wheelbarrow is a humble tool rather than a conventionally elevated poetic subject. By placing it at the center of attention, Williams suggests that daily life depends on objects whose value is usually taken for granted.

### Perception and attention

The poem slows the act of seeing. Red, white, rain, and the wheelbarrow’s surface are isolated and reassembled so that the familiar scene becomes newly strange and precise.

### Labor and interdependence

The farm setting hints at a network of practical relationships among tools, weather, animals, and people. “Depends” names that network without specifying one final answer, keeping the poem open to the reader’s experience.

## Form and meter

The poem is free verse rather than a fixed metrical form. Its sixteen words are arranged in four couplets, each made of a longer first line followed by a short second line.

Williams’s lineation breaks compound words across stanza lines: “wheel / barrow” and “rain / water.” These pauses make the reader encounter the parts of the image separately before recognizing the whole.

There is no punctuation. The syntax remains one continuous sentence, while the stanza breaks create visual pauses. The result is both fragmented and connected: each image stands apart, yet all four units belong to the same scene.

## Literary devices

### Imagery

> a red wheel / barrow ... the white / chickens

The poem relies on exact visual details rather than explanation. The red-and-white contrast and the rain-glazed surface make the scene concrete enough to be seen before it is interpreted.

### Enjambment and word division

> glazed with rain / water

Breaking “rainwater” across lines slows the compound word and gives rain and water separate emphasis. The unusual spacing turns typography into part of the act of looking.

### Ambiguity

> so much depends / upon

The opening states importance without naming its cause or consequence. That missing object of “depends” invites multiple readings while keeping the poem anchored in the physical image that follows.

### Juxtaposition

> a red wheelbarrow ... the white chickens

The utilitarian tool is set beside living farm animals and natural rain. Their proximity suggests a shared environment without forcing the objects into a single allegorical meaning.

## Historical context

The poem was first published in 1923 in Williams’s experimental collection Spring and All. Its plain diction, concrete image, and rejection of conventional meter place it within the modernist turn toward direct, everyday American speech.

Williams was both a physician and a poet, and his work repeatedly makes local scenes, working people, and ordinary objects subjects for serious poetry. The wheelbarrow poem is especially compressed: almost all of its language after the opening two lines describes one image.

The poem is often discussed alongside Imagist practice because it privileges a precise image, economy of language, and the reader’s direct encounter with things. Its ambiguity does not cancel that precision; it makes the image the basis from which interpretation begins.

## What critics say

> “Williams’s famous maxim, “No ideas but in things,” helps explain how the poem grounds ideas and emotions in the concrete world rather than stating an abstract argument.”
>
> — Craig Morgan Teicher, [Craig Morgan Teicher, “William Carlos Williams: ‘The Red Wheelbarrow’”](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/articles/68731/william-carlos-williams-the-red-wheelbarrow)

> “The poem’s separate stanzas and absent punctuation create a tension between independence and connection, so that form and content become part of the poem’s meaning.”
>
> — [Academy of American Poets, “On ‘The Red Wheelbarrow’”](https://poets.org/text/red-wheelbarrow)

## Common questions

### What is the meaning of “The Red Wheelbarrow”?

The poem makes an ordinary wheelbarrow feel essential without explaining exactly what depends on it. It asks readers to consider how work, life, and meaning can rest on overlooked physical things.

### How is “The Red Wheelbarrow” an Imagist poem?

It uses economical language and a precise concrete image instead of abstract explanation or decorative description. Its red wheelbarrow, rainwater, and white chickens carry the poem’s significance through direct perception.

### Why does Williams break “wheelbarrow” and “rainwater” across lines?

The breaks make the reader pause over each part of the compound words. They emphasize the material details and make the poem’s visual arrangement part of its meaning.

### What does “so much depends upon” mean?

The phrase deliberately leaves its object unstated. It can suggest practical dependence on a farm tool, but it also makes the reader notice how much interpretation depends on the concrete image placed before us.

## References

- [The Red Wheelbarrow: poem text](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/45502/the-red-wheelbarrow) — The Poetry Foundation

- [William Carlos Williams: “The Red Wheelbarrow”](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/articles/68731/william-carlos-williams-the-red-wheelbarrow) — The Poetry Foundation

- [On “The Red Wheelbarrow”](https://poets.org/text/red-wheelbarrow) — Academy of American Poets

# The Rime of the Ancient Mariner analysis

The Rime of the Ancient Mariner — Samuel Taylor Coleridge (1798)

Samuel Taylor Coleridge's The Rime of the Ancient Mariner turns an inexplicable act at sea into a haunting study of guilt, nature, and attempted redemption. This analysis explains its meaning, themes, form, and symbolism.

## The poem

```
It is an ancyent Marinere,
And he stoppeth one of three:
“By thy long grey beard and glittering eye
Now wherefore stopp’st thou me?

The Bridegroom’s doors are open’d wide,
And I am next of kin;
The Guests are met, the Feast is set,—
May’st hear the merry din.”

He holds him with his glittering eye—
The Wedding-Guest stood still,
And listens like a three years’ child:
The Marinere hath his will.

The Wedding-Guest sate on a stone:
He cannot chuse but hear;
And thus spake on that ancient man,
The bright-eyed Mariner.

The ship was cheered, the harbour cleared,
Merrily did we drop
Below the kirk, below the hill,
Below the lighthouse top.

The Ice was here, the Ice was there,
The Ice was all around:
It crack’d and growl’d, and roar’d and howl’d—
Like noises in a swound!

At length did cross an Albatross,
Thorough the Fog it came;
And an it were a Christian Soul,
We hail’d it in God’s name.

The Marineres gave it biscuit-worms,
And round and round it flew:
The Ice did split with a Thunder-fit;
The Helmsman steer’d us thro’.

And a good south wind sprung up behind;
The Albatross did follow;
And every day, for food or play,
Came to the Marinere’s hollo!

In mist or cloud, on mast or shroud,
It perch’d for vespers nine;
Whiles all the night, through fog-smoke white,
Glimmer’d the white Moon-shine.

“God save thee, ancyent Marinere!
From the fiends that plague thee thus!
Why look’st thou so?”—With my cross-bow
I shot the Albatross.
```

This excerpt presents the frame narrative, the voyage into the ice, the albatross's arrival and welcome, and the Mariner's unexplained shooting of the bird. The complete seven-part poem is available at the linked 1798 text source.

Text from [The Rime of the Ancyent Marinere (1798)](https://en.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=The_Rime_of_the_Ancyent_Marinere_%281798%29). Public domain in the US (First published in Lyrical Ballads in 1798; works first published in the United States by 1930 are public domain.).

## Summary

An ancient mariner stops a wedding guest and compels him to hear a sea story. After the ship reaches ice and fog, an albatross appears, and the crew welcomes it as a Christian soul.

The mariner suddenly kills the harmless bird with his crossbow. That unexplained act begins the poem's supernatural ordeal, in which the crew suffers, the mariner bears the albatross as a sign of guilt, and his later blessing of living creatures begins an incomplete process of penance.

## Meaning and interpretation

The poem's meaning is not exhausted by the simple lesson that the mariner should not have killed the albatross. The act is arbitrary: the narrative gives no motive, which makes the resulting guilt feel like an encounter with mortality, responsibility, and consequences that cannot be neatly explained.

Coleridge's poem holds moral clarity and imaginative ambiguity together. The mariner eventually says that prayer is bound to loving “man and bird and beast,” but his endless compulsion to retell the story shows that recognition does not erase harm or restore him to his former life.

## Themes

### Guilt and penance

The dead albatross becomes a visible sign of an act whose consequences fall on the whole crew. The mariner's punishment is not a single sentence completed once, but a recurring obligation to tell the tale.

### Nature and spiritual interdependence

The albatross is both a living animal and a figure the sailors interpret through religious language. The poem links violence toward the natural world with spiritual disorder, then makes renewed attention to living creatures part of the mariner's recovery.

### The supernatural and the unknowable

Storms, spirits, Death, and Life-in-Death create a world that exceeds ordinary explanation. Rather than making every event clear, the supernatural intensifies the poem's questions about why suffering follows an apparently senseless choice.

### Storytelling and compulsion

The mariner's story interrupts a wedding and changes the wedding guest. His repeated retellings make narrative both a burden and the only form of witness available to him.

## Form and meter

The poem is a supernatural narrative ballad arranged in seven parts. Its short stanzas, repeated phrases, dialogue, archaic diction, and abrupt changes of scene create the feeling of an oral tale being performed.

Much of the poem draws on alternating four-stress and three-stress ballad lines, but Coleridge varies line length, syntax, rhyme, and rhythm extensively. The irregularity suits a story that moves between ordinary speech, incantation, nightmare, and theological reflection.

The 1798 first edition differs from later versions, especially the 1817 text with its marginal glosses. This excerpt follows the 1798 Lyrical Ballads spelling and punctuation rather than silently combining editions.

## Literary devices

### Frame narrative

> He holds him with his glittering eye—

The mariner's interruption of the wedding guest creates a story within a story. The guest's forced attention also gives the reader a character whose response registers the tale's psychological effect.

### Symbolism

> I shot the Albatross.

The albatross becomes a symbol of violated life, arbitrary guilt, and the burden of consequence. Its meaning expands as the mariner's punishment continues beyond the original act.

### Repetition and refrain

> The Ice was here, the Ice was there,

Repetition turns description into incantation and emphasizes confinement. Recurrent formulas also echo oral ballad traditions while making the voyage feel cyclical and inescapable.

### Simile and sound imagery

> Like noises in a swound!

The ice is made audible through verbs such as “crack’d,” “growl’d,” “roar’d,” and “howl’d.” The comparison to a swoon blurs physical weather and altered consciousness.

## Historical context

The poem first appeared in the 1798 edition of Lyrical Ballads, the collaborative volume associated with Coleridge and William Wordsworth and often treated as a landmark of British Romantic poetry.

Coleridge revised the poem repeatedly. The 1817 version is especially recognizable for its marginal glosses, while the first edition uses the title and spellings “The Rime of the Ancyent Marinere.” This page identifies the 1798 publication while making the edition of the excerpt explicit.

The poem's sea voyage, polar ice, supernatural punishment, and archaic ballad voice combine older literary conventions with Romantic interest in intense feeling, imagination, and the relation between human beings and the natural world.

## What critics say

> “The remarkable thing about the poem is its analysis of a sense of guilt without a corresponding sense of willful wrongdoing.”
>
> — Adam Roberts, [Literary Theory and Criticism](https://literariness.org/2021/02/16/analysis-of-coleridges-the-rime-of-the-ancient-mariner/)

> “The narrative of the poem and the marginal gloss are often in conflict with each other, creating a dynamic of tension.”
>
> — Claudia Stumpf, [Inquire: Journal of Comparative Literature](https://inquire.streetmag.org/articles/82)

> “The poem, then, casts the appreciation and valuing of nature, the act of embracing Romanticism, not just as important in and of itself, but as above all a spiritual, religious necessity.”
>
> — [LitCharts](https://www.litcharts.com/lit/rime-of-the-ancient-mariner/themes/the-natural-and-the-spiritual)

## Common questions

### What is the main meaning of The Rime of the Ancient Mariner?

The poem examines guilt, responsibility, and the difficult possibility of redemption after the mariner kills an albatross for no stated reason. It connects spiritual recovery with learning to value living things, while leaving the supernatural causes of the punishment partly mysterious.

### What does the albatross symbolize?

The albatross symbolizes living nature, violated innocence, and the burden of consequence. Once the mariner kills it, the bird becomes a public sign of guilt and a reminder that his action has affected more than himself.

### What are the main themes in the poem?

The central themes include guilt and penance, humanity's relationship with nature, the supernatural, and the compulsive power of storytelling. The poem also explores how moral meaning can coexist with uncertainty.

### What form and meter does The Rime of the Ancient Mariner use?

It is a seven-part supernatural narrative ballad. Much of its verse uses alternating four-stress and three-stress lines, but Coleridge varies the rhythm, rhyme, stanza shape, and line length, so it is better treated as an irregular ballad form than as a single strict meter.

## References

- [The Rime of the Ancyent Marinere (1798) — full text](https://en.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=The_Rime_of_the_Ancyent_Marinere_%281798%29) — Wikisource

- [Analysis of Coleridge's The Rime of the Ancient Mariner](https://literariness.org/2021/02/16/analysis-of-coleridges-the-rime-of-the-ancient-mariner/) — Literary Theory and Criticism

- [The Natural and the Spiritual Theme](https://www.litcharts.com/lit/rime-of-the-ancient-mariner/themes/the-natural-and-the-spiritual) — LitCharts

# The River-Merchant's Wife: A Letter analysis

The River-Merchant's Wife: A Letter — Ezra Pound, after Li Bai (1915)

This analysis explains how Ezra Pound's translation uses childhood memory, precise natural images, and free verse to portray love deepened by separation.

## The poem

```
While my hair was still cut straight across my forehead
I played about the front gate, pulling flowers.
You came by on bamboo stilts, playing horse,
You walked about my seat, playing with blue plums.
And we went on living in the village of Chokan:
Two small people, without dislike or suspicion.

At fourteen I married My Lord you.
I never laughed, being bashful.
Lowering my head, I looked at the wall.
Called to, a thousand times, I never looked back.

At fifteen I stopped scowling,
I desired my dust to be mingled with yours
Forever and forever, and forever.
Why should I climb the look out?

At sixteen you departed,
You went into far Ku-to-Yen, by the river of swirling eddies,
And you have been gone five months.
The monkeys make sorrowful noise overhead.

You dragged your feet when you went out.
By the gate now, the moss is grown, the different mosses,
Too deep to clear them away!
The leaves fall early this autumn, in wind.
The paired butterflies are already yellow with August
Over the grass in the West garden,
They hurt me,
I grow older,
If you are coming down through the narrows of the river Kiang,
Please let me know beforehand,
And I will come out to meet you,
As far as Cho-fu-Sa.
```

Text from [Cathay](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/50155/50155-h/50155-h.htm). Public domain in the US (Pound's English translation was first published in Cathay in 1915, before January 1, 1931, and the source text is identified as public domain in the United States.).

## Summary

The speaker addresses her absent husband by remembering the relationship from childhood. Their playful closeness becomes marriage, and marriage becomes a painful period of waiting after he leaves on a commercial journey.

The poem's emotional movement is gradual rather than dramatic: affection grows through shared history, while the abandoned home gathers moss and autumn. The final request asks for advance notice of his return, but the reunion remains only imagined.

## Meaning and interpretation

The poem presents separation as a way of discovering the depth of love. The speaker first recalls a childhood without suspicion, then describes the desire for her dust to be mingled with his. Her present loneliness makes those ordinary memories newly intense.

Pound's version is best read as a translation and a modernist re-creation, not as a transparent equivalent of Li Bai's Chinese poem. The concrete images and compressed transitions make an ancient emotional situation immediate in English, while the mediation through Ernest Fenollosa's notes raises questions about what translation preserves and what it changes.

## Themes

### Love and separation

The speaker's account moves from games at the gate to married devotion and then to absence. The husband's departure gives the earlier scenes their emotional weight: remembered play becomes evidence of a bond she cannot replace.

### Time and changing identity

The repeated ages—fourteen, fifteen, and sixteen—organize the speaker's growth. The final statement, “I grow older,” compresses the five months of waiting into a larger awareness that love, marriage, and selfhood are changing together.

### Nature as emotional reflection

Moss, falling leaves, autumn butterflies, and sorrowful monkeys turn the landscape into a register of waiting. Nature does not simply mirror the speaker's feeling; its seasonal change makes absence visible and measurable.

### Translation and cultural mediation

The names “Rihaku,” “Chokan,” and “Ku-to-Yen” signal the poem's route through Chinese material, Japanese forms, Fenollosa's notes, and Pound's English. Its power as an English poem and its distance from the source tradition should be considered together.

## Form and meter

The poem is written in free verse, with no fixed rhyme scheme or regular metrical pattern. Its uneven stanza lengths and conversational syntax make the poem feel like a letter spoken from memory rather than a formally closed lyric.

Pound gives each line a strong image or syntactic movement: bamboo stilts, blue plums, moss, butterflies, and the river. Repetition—especially “Forever and forever, and forever”—creates rhythm without imposing a traditional meter.

The five uneven stanzas move from childhood recollection to marriage, devotion, departure, and the long final scene of waiting. The final conditional request leaves the poem emotionally open: the speaker plans a meeting, but does not receive an answer.

## Literary devices

### Concrete imagery

> You came by on bamboo stilts, playing horse,

The bamboo stilts and blue plums make the remembered courtship tactile and visible. Such objects carry the relationship more effectively than abstract declarations would.

### Anaphora and repetition

> At fourteen... / At fifteen... / At sixteen...

The repeated age markers give the speaker's story a simple chronology. The repetition of “forever” then stretches that chronology toward a promise that the present separation tests.

### Seasonal symbolism

> The leaves fall early this autumn, in wind.

Autumn suggests decline and the passage of time, while the early leaf-fall makes the speaker's waiting seem premature and unnatural. The season becomes part of the pressure of absence.

### Personification

> The monkeys make sorrowful noise overhead.

The monkeys' sound is described through the speaker's sorrow. Their cries seem to join her lament, showing how grief can transform ordinary sounds into emotional evidence.

## Historical context

Ezra Pound published Cathay in 1915. Its title page described the poems as translations “for the most part from the Chinese of Rihaku,” Pound's form of Li Bai's name. The River-Merchant's Wife: A Letter is based on Li Bai's eighth-century poem Changgan Xing.

Pound worked from Ernest Fenollosa's notes and from decipherings by Professors Mori and Ariga rather than translating directly from Chinese. Yale's Modernism Lab notes that Pound was not proficient in Chinese and often altered or omitted details while shaping the material into a new English poem.

The poem appeared during the First World War. Hugh Kenner's reading of Cathay as a book of war poetry places its stories of departure, exile, and waiting in a wider culture of separation, although that interpretation remains debated.

## What critics say

> “The “real achievement” of Cathay, according to Kenner, “lay not on the frontier of comparative poetics, but securely within the effort…to rethink the nature of an English poem.””
>
> — Hugh Kenner, quoted by Andrew Karas, [Yale Modernism Lab](https://campuspress.yale.edu/modernismlab/cathay/)

> “The poems in Cathay might be more profitably considered translations of certain states of mind or modes of existence than of specific words on a page.”
>
> — Andrew Karas, [Yale Modernism Lab](https://campuspress.yale.edu/modernismlab/cathay/)

> “It explores themes of love, loss, and separation.”
>
> — [Poem Analysis](https://poemanalysis.com/ezra-pound/the-river-merchants-wife-a-letter/)

## Common questions

### What is the main meaning of The River-Merchant's Wife: A Letter?

The poem shows how separation reveals and intensifies love. The speaker's memories of childhood and marriage become more painful as the absent husband and the changing seasons make time tangible.

### What are the main themes of the poem?

The main themes are love, separation, time, memory, and nature. The poem also invites questions about translation because Pound re-created Li Bai's poem through Fenollosa's notes.

### What form does The River-Merchant's Wife: A Letter use?

It uses free verse, with uneven stanzas, no fixed rhyme scheme, and no regular meter. Repeated ages, images, and phrases provide structure in place of a traditional pattern.

### Is Pound's poem a direct translation of Li Bai?

No. It is a loose translation or re-creation based on Fenollosa's notes and other decipherings. It is valuable as a modernist English poem, but it should not be treated as a word-for-word rendering of the Chinese original.

## References

- [Cathay full text](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/50155/50155-h/50155-h.htm) — Project Gutenberg

- [The River Merchant's Wife: A Letter text and public-domain note](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_River_Merchant%27s_Wife:_A_Letter) — Wikisource

- [Cathay and modernist translation](https://campuspress.yale.edu/modernismlab/cathay/) — Yale Modernism Lab

# The Road Not Taken analysis

The Road Not Taken — Robert Frost (1916)

Robert Frost's The Road Not Taken is often read as advice to choose an unconventional path. A close reading shows a more unsettled poem about similar choices, regret, and the stories we tell afterward.

## The poem

```
Two roads diverged in a yellow wood,
And sorry I could not travel both
And be one traveler, long I stood
And looked down one as far as I could
To where it bent in the undergrowth;

Then took the other, as just as fair,
And having perhaps the better claim,
Because it was grassy and wanted wear;
Though as for that the passing there
Had worn them really about the same,

And both that morning equally lay
In leaves no step had trodden black.
Oh, I kept the first for another day!
Yet knowing how way leads on to way,
I doubted if I should ever come back.

I shall be telling this with a sigh
Somewhere ages and ages hence:
Two roads diverged in a wood, and I—
I took the one less traveled by,
And that has made all the difference.
```

Text from [The Road Not Taken — Poetry Foundation](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/44272/the-road-not-taken). Public domain in the US (First published in 1915 and collected in Mountain Interval in 1916; works first published in the United States by 1930 are public domain.).

## Summary

A traveler reaches two roads in an autumn wood and cannot inspect either one beyond the point where it bends. He chooses one, initially describing it as slightly less worn, then immediately admits that the roads were worn about the same.

The final stanza imagines the traveler retelling the choice in the distant future. The poem leaves the meaning of the final “difference” open: it may be satisfaction, regret, or the significance created by hindsight.

## Meaning and interpretation

The poem is not simply an instruction to take the road less traveled. Its central tension comes from the contradiction between that famous claim and the earlier observation that the two roads were “really about the same.” The speaker makes a choice without enough information to know that one path is better, then imagines a future story that gives the choice a clear meaning.

That story may be sincere, ironic, or both. Frost's poem keeps the speaker's “sigh” emotionally ambiguous, so the ending can hold pride and regret at once. Choice changes the speaker's future, but the poem questions whether the chosen road was inherently special.

## Themes

### Choice and irreversibility

The traveler wants to keep the first road for another day, but knows that one way leads to another and doubts he will return. Choosing one possibility closes off direct knowledge of the other.

### Hindsight and self-narration

The future retelling turns an uncertain decision into a compact life story. The poem examines how people assign significance to choices after the outcomes are already part of their lives.

### Regret and ambiguity

The repeated attention to the untaken road and the unresolved “sigh” keep regret present. The ending does not say whether the difference was fortunate, unfortunate, or simply consequential.

## Form and meter

The poem has four five-line stanzas, or quatrains with a final short line, and an ABAAB rhyme scheme in each stanza.

Its base is iambic tetrameter: four rising beats per line. Frost varies the conversational rhythm with substitutions, extra syllables, pauses, and syntactic turns, so the meter supports speech rather than sounding mechanically regular.

The long first sentence runs across the opening three stanzas, mirroring deliberation and revision. The final stanza shifts into a stylized future story, where the repeated “I” makes the choice sound more dramatic than the scene itself.

## Literary devices

### Extended metaphor

> Two roads diverged in a yellow wood,

The fork in the wood becomes a sustained metaphor for alternatives in a life. The concrete setting also limits the metaphor: both paths are ordinary roads, not visibly moral or heroic destinies.

### Irony

> I took the one less traveled by,

The line sounds like a declaration of independence, but the preceding lines say that the passing had worn the roads about the same. The apparent advice is undercut by the poem's own evidence.

### Repetition

> And be one traveler

Repeated words such as “And,” “road,” and “I” make the speaker's thought circle back. “One traveler” emphasizes the desire to experience both alternatives without being divided by choice.

### Ambiguous symbolism

> I shall be telling this with a sigh

The sigh can suggest relief, regret, amusement, or self-dramatization. Because Frost does not resolve it, the final image resists a single symbolic lesson.

## Historical context

Frost wrote the poem in 1915, and it appeared as the opening poem of his 1916 collection Mountain Interval. The Poetry Foundation connects its setting to a period when Europe was at war and many people doubted they would return to what they had left.

Frost wrote the poem as a joke for his friend Edward Thomas, who often regretted whichever path the two men chose on their walks. Thomas initially missed the joke, and Frost later described the final sigh as “mock” and “hypo-critical for the fun of the thing.”

## What critics say

> “choosing one rather than the other was a matter of impulse, impossible to speak about any more clearly than to say that the road taken had “perhaps the better claim.””
>
> — William Pritchard, [The Poetry Foundation](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/articles/89511/robert-frost-the-road-not-taken)

> “Which road, after all, is the road “not taken”?”
>
> — Mark Richardson, [Academy of American Poets](https://poets.org/text/road-not-taken-poem-everyone-loves-and-everyone-gets-wrong)

## Common questions

### What is the main meaning of The Road Not Taken?

It explores how people choose between uncertain alternatives and later create stories about those choices. The poem does not clearly say that one road was better.

### Is The Road Not Taken about choosing the less-traveled path?

Not simply. The speaker first says the chosen road looked grassy, but then says the two roads were worn “really about the same.” The famous final claim may be a retrospective, partly ironic story rather than direct advice.

### What meter does The Road Not Taken use?

Its underlying pattern is mostly iambic tetrameter, four iambic feet per line, with natural variations in stress, syllable count, and phrasing.

### Why does the speaker sigh?

The sigh is deliberately ambiguous. It can express regret, satisfaction, wistfulness, or the theatrical distance of someone turning an ordinary decision into a life story.

## References

- [The Road Not Taken — full poem](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/44272/the-road-not-taken) — The Poetry Foundation

- [Robert Frost: “The Road Not Taken”](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/articles/89511/robert-frost-the-road-not-taken) — The Poetry Foundation

- [The Road Not Taken: The Poem Everyone Loves and Everyone Gets Wrong](https://poets.org/text/road-not-taken-poem-everyone-loves-and-everyone-gets-wrong) — Academy of American Poets

## Open the editor

Write with this poem’s meter in the editor: https://lyriic.com/write

# The Second Coming analysis

The Second Coming — William Butler Yeats (1920)

This analysis explains how Yeats turns a falcon’s lost command, a widening gyre, and a sphinx-like rough beast into a vision of civilization entering a terrifying new cycle.

## The poem

```
Turning and turning in the widening gyre
The falcon cannot hear the falconer;
Things fall apart; the centre cannot hold;
Mere anarchy is loosed upon the world,
The blood-dimmed tide is loosed, and everywhere
The ceremony of innocence is drowned;
The best lack all conviction, while the worst
Are full of passionate intensity.

Surely some revelation is at hand;
Surely the Second Coming is at hand.
The Second Coming! Hardly are those words out
When a vast image out of Spiritus Mundi
Troubles my sight: somewhere in sands of the desert
A shape with lion body and the head of a man,
A gaze blank and pitiless as the sun,
Is moving its slow thighs, while all about it
Reel shadows of the indignant desert birds.
The darkness drops again; but now I know
That twenty centuries of stony sleep
Were vexed to nightmare by a rocking cradle,
And what rough beast, its hour come round at last,
Slouches towards Bethlehem to be born?
```

Text from [The Second Coming](https://celt.ucc.ie/published/E910001-066.html). Public domain in the US (First published in The Dial in November 1920; the poem is in the US public domain.).

## Summary

The first stanza describes a world losing its organizing centre. A falcon has flown beyond the falconer’s call, anarchy and violence spread, innocence is drowned, and the people best equipped to resist seem passive while destructive forces act with energy.

The speaker expects a Christian revelation, but the vision that arrives is a desert creature with a lion’s body and a man’s head. The poem ends by asking what rough beast is moving toward Bethlehem to begin the next historical age.

## Meaning and interpretation

The widening gyre is both a literal spiral and an image of Yeats’s cyclical theory of history. As the falcon moves beyond the falconer’s hearing, the relationship between motion and control breaks down; the image becomes a compact metaphor for a civilization no longer governed by its former principles.

“Things fall apart; the centre cannot hold” compresses political, moral, and spiritual collapse into one memorable statement. The following blood tide and drowned ceremony make the crisis collective: innocence is not simply lost by individuals but overwhelmed by forces moving through the world.

The second stanza revises the expected Christian Second Coming. Instead of a savior, the speaker sees a pitiless hybrid whose arrival is an anti-Nativity. Yeats leaves the beast’s identity unresolved, so it can signify the violent, dehumanized historical force born when an old order reaches its limit.

## Themes

### Historical cycles and the gyre

Yeats’s gyre is a spiral or vortex that represents a phase of history expanding toward crisis. The poem catches one cycle at the point where its centre can no longer contain the forces it has released.

### The collapse of authority

The falcon cannot hear the falconer, and the best lack conviction. Communication, leadership, and moral confidence all fail at once, leaving passionate intensity to the worst actors.

### Apocalypse and reversed revelation

The title invokes Christian prophecy, but the revelation is frightening rather than redemptive. Bethlehem becomes the destination of a new birth whose consequences are unknown and ominous.

## Form and meter

The poem has two stanzas: an eight-line opening and a fourteen-line second stanza. The second stanza’s sonnet-like length does not produce a conventional sonnet structure; the poem’s form feels deliberately unstable as the vision exceeds containment.

It is often described as blank verse, but the iambic pentameter is irregular. The opening lines use substitutions and extra syllables, while the vision’s long syntactic units strain the meter. This pressure makes formal instability echo the poem’s collapsing order.

There is no settled end-rhyme scheme. Near-rhymes and repeated sounds create partial links without restoring a neat pattern, while enjambment carries the reader through the tide, vision, and final question.

## Literary devices

### Symbolism

> Turning and turning in the widening gyre

The gyre symbolizes Yeats’s cyclical movement of history. Its widening motion suggests expansion away from a stable centre and toward a violent transition.

### Extended metaphor

> The falcon cannot hear the falconer

The falcon’s separation from its trainer turns a familiar image of control into a picture of failed communication and a civilization that has exceeded its guiding authority.

### Allusion and inversion

> Surely the Second Coming is at hand

The title and Bethlehem invoke Christian eschatology and the birth of Christ. The expected savior is replaced by an unnamed beast, making the poem’s revelation a dark inversion of the Nativity.

### Apostrophe and repetition

> Surely some revelation is at hand; / Surely the Second Coming is at hand.

The repeated “Surely” sounds like insistence mixed with desperation. Repetition briefly creates expectation before the speaker’s vision overturns it.

### Rhetorical question

> And what rough beast, its hour come round at last, / Slouches towards Bethlehem to be born?

The closing question refuses to name or explain the beast. Its slow verb and unanswered syntax leave the new age approaching rather than completed.

## Historical context

Yeats wrote the poem in January 1919, amid the aftermath of World War I, political unrest in Ireland, and the influenza pandemic. It was first published in The Dial in November 1920 and later appeared in Michael Robartes and the Dancer (1921).

The poem draws on Yeats’s mystical system of interlocking gyres, developed most fully in A Vision. In that framework, historical eras move through cycles; the poem imagines the Christian era’s two thousand years reaching a moment of violent transition.

The poem’s references to Spiritus Mundi, Bethlehem, and a new birth combine occult, biblical, and mythic language. The result is not a precise political forecast but an intentionally open image that later readers can apply to different crises.

## What critics say

> “The poem reveals, in other words, an order, a twisted logic behind the apparent disorder of the contemporary world”
>
> — Adrian Paterson, [Adrian Paterson, Moore Institute](https://mooreinstitute.ie/2020/12/18/9809/)

> “the gyre is an image Yeats uses to symbolize grand, sweeping historical movements as a kind of spiral”
>
> — [LitCharts, “The Second Coming”](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/william-butler-yeats/the-second-coming)

## Common questions

### What is the main meaning of “The Second Coming”?

Yeats presents a civilization losing its moral and political centre as one historical cycle ends. The expected Christian renewal is replaced by the frightening arrival of an unknown rough beast.

### What does the gyre mean in “The Second Coming”?

The gyre is a spiral image for Yeats’s theory that history moves through recurring cycles. The widening gyre suggests an era moving away from its centre and toward upheaval.

### What does “Things fall apart; the centre cannot hold” mean?

The line means that the forces holding society together have failed. Order, authority, shared values, and communication can no longer contain the violence spreading through the world.

### Who or what is the rough beast?

The rough beast is a deliberately ambiguous, sphinx-like figure with a lion’s body and a man’s head. It represents the brutal new force or historical era that may emerge after the collapse of the old one.

## References

- [Poem text and publication history](https://celt.ucc.ie/published/E910001-066.html) — University College Cork, Corpus of Electronic Texts

- [Rereading “The Second Coming”](https://mooreinstitute.ie/2020/12/18/9809/) — Moore Institute, University of Galway

- [“The Second Coming” analysis and form notes](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/william-butler-yeats/the-second-coming) — LitCharts

# The Song of Hiawatha analysis

The Song of Hiawatha — Henry Wadsworth Longfellow (1855)

Explore The Song of Hiawatha through its famous opening, musical trochaic tetrameter, and layered treatment of story, place, and cultural memory.

## The poem

```
Should you ask me, whence these stories?
Whence these legends and traditions,
With the odors of the forest
With the dew and damp of meadows,
With the curling smoke of wigwams,
With the rushing of great rivers,
With their frequent repetitions,
And their wild reverberations
As of thunder in the mountains?

I should answer, I should tell you,
“From the forests and the prairies,
From the great lakes of the Northland,
From the land of the Ojibways,
From the land of the Dacotahs,
From the mountains, moors, and fen-lands
Where the heron, the Shuh-shuh-gah,
Feeds among the reeds and rushes.
I repeat them as I heard them
From the lips of Nawadaha,
The musician, the sweet singer.”

Should you ask where Nawadaha
Found these songs so wild and wayward,
Found these legends and traditions,
I should answer, I should tell you,
“In the bird’s-nests of the forest,
In the lodges of the beaver,
In the hoofprint of the bison,
In the eyry of the eagle!
All the wild-fowl sang them to him,
In the moorlands and the fen-lands,
In the melancholy marshes;
Chetowaik, the plover, sang them,
Mahng, the loon, the wild-goose, Wawa,
The blue heron, the Shuh-shuh-gah,
And the grouse, the Mushkodasa!”
```

This excerpt is the opening Introduction, where the speaker presents the poem as a song received from landscapes, animals, and the Ojibwe and Dacotah lands. Read the complete poem at Project Gutenberg.

Text from [The Song of Hiawatha](https://gutenberg.org/files/19/19-h/19-h.htm). Public domain in the US (First published in 1855, The Song of Hiawatha is in the public domain in the United States.).

## Summary

In the Introduction, the speaker answers questions about the origin of the poem’s stories. He places them in forests, prairies, lakes, and the “land of the Ojibways” and says that Nawadaha received them from birds and the natural world.

The opening therefore frames The Song of Hiawatha as a performed or transmitted legend rather than a private invention. Its repetitions and musical cadence make the act of listening part of the poem’s subject.

## Meaning and interpretation

The Introduction presents cultural memory as something carried through voice, landscape, and living creatures. The speaker’s repeated “I should answer” sounds like a storyteller welcoming an audience into an inherited tradition.

That framing is also historically complicated. Longfellow adapted materials associated with Henry Schoolcraft and shaped them into a nineteenth-century American epic; the poem’s lyrical respect for Indigenous traditions exists alongside the limits and stereotypes of that mediation.

## Themes

### Storytelling and cultural memory

The poem begins by explaining where its legends came from and by naming a chain of transmission: the speaker, Nawadaha, birds, and the land. Repetition gives the opening the feel of an oral performance.

### Nature as archive

Forests, rivers, marshes, animal tracks, and birds’ nests function as repositories of story. The natural world is not merely scenery; it is imagined as an active source and witness of tradition.

### Cultural representation and its limits

The Introduction announces an attempt to center Indigenous legends in a popular American poem, but modern readers must also ask who is speaking, collecting, and reshaping those traditions for a predominantly white audience.

## Form and meter

The Song of Hiawatha is a long narrative poem organized into an Introduction and twenty-two sections. This page uses the opening Introduction as an excerpt.

Longfellow writes in trochaic tetrameter: four falling feet, usually a stressed syllable followed by an unstressed syllable. The steady beat supports the poem’s chant-like storytelling and its frequent repetitions.

The poem relies more on rhythm, parallel phrasing, and recurring sounds than on a fixed end-rhyme scheme. The repeated questions and answers create a call-and-response movement.

## Literary devices

### Anaphora and repetition

> “Should you ask me”

The repeated question-and-answer structure establishes an oral frame and makes the reader feel addressed directly. Repetition also turns the opening into a memorable performance.

### Personification

> “All the wild-fowl sang them to him”

Birds are given the role of singers and transmitters. This makes nature part of the poem’s imagined community of storytellers.

### Sensory imagery

> “With the curling smoke of wigwams”

Smell, moisture, sight, and sound build a physical landscape before the narrative begins. The legends seem to arise from a whole environment rather than from an abstract past.

### Parallelism

> “From the forests and the prairies, / From the great lakes of the Northland”

The repeated grammatical pattern maps the story across a widening geography. It also gives the lines a balanced, ceremonial rhythm.

## Historical context

Longfellow completed The Song of Hiawatha in 1855, and it was published on November 10 of that year. The Project Gutenberg introductory note says that Longfellow based the poem on material associated especially with Henry Rowe Schoolcraft’s studies of Ojibwe traditions.

Longfellow openly acknowledged using the meter of the Finnish Kalevala, while the poem’s sources and representation of Indigenous cultures have drawn continuing criticism. The National Park Service describes the work as both an effort to honor Native American heritage and a poem that perpetuated stereotypes and the idea that Indigenous culture was disappearing.

## What critics say

> ““In this epic work, Longfellow set out to honor Native American heritage, but simultaneously perpetuated stereotypes and the false assertion that Indigenous culture was dying in America.””
>
> — [Longfellow House Washington’s Headquarters National Historic Site](https://www.nps.gov/long/learn/historyculture/hiawatha.htm)

> ““Longfellow used rhythmic poetry to convey various Native American myths to a popular audience.””
>
> — [Longfellow House Washington’s Headquarters National Historic Site](https://www.nps.gov/long/learn/historyculture/hiawatha.htm)

> ““Longfellow made no secret of the fact that he had used the meter of the Kalevala; but as for the legends, he openly gave credit to Schoolcraft in his notes to the poem.””
>
> — [Project Gutenberg introductory note](https://gutenberg.org/files/19/19-h/19-h.htm)

## Common questions

### What is the meaning of The Song of Hiawatha’s Introduction?

The Introduction presents the poem as a chain of oral and natural transmission. Its stories come from landscapes, animals, and Indigenous traditions, then reach the reader through the singer Nawadaha and the poem’s speaker.

### What is The Song of Hiawatha about?

It is a long narrative about the legendary hero Hiawatha, his origins, adventures, relationships, and eventual departure. The poem combines Indigenous legends associated with Schoolcraft with Longfellow’s own literary design.

### What meter does The Song of Hiawatha use?

The poem is written primarily in trochaic tetrameter, a four-beat falling rhythm. Repetition, parallel phrasing, and the regular pulse give its narration a chant-like quality.

### Why is The Song of Hiawatha historically controversial?

Longfellow brought Indigenous characters and traditions into a widely read American epic, but he also filtered them through nineteenth-century sources and assumptions. Modern readings therefore consider both the poem’s cultural impact and its stereotypes and assimilationist framing.

## References

- [The Song of Hiawatha](https://gutenberg.org/files/19/19-h/19-h.htm) — Project Gutenberg

- [Hiawatha](https://www.nps.gov/long/learn/historyculture/hiawatha.htm) — National Park Service

# The Song of Wandering Aengus analysis

The Song of Wandering Aengus — W. B. Yeats (1899)

W. B. Yeats's The Song of Wandering Aengus follows a magical encounter into a lifelong search for beauty, love, and an ideal that may never be reached. This analysis explains the poem's meaning, themes, imagery, and form.

## The poem

```
I went out to the hazel wood,
Because a fire was in my head,
And cut and peeled a hazel wand,
And hooked a berry to a thread;
And when white moths were on the wing,
And moth-like stars were flickering out,
I dropped the berry in a stream
And caught a little silver trout.

When I had laid it on the floor
I went to blow the fire a-flame,
But something rustled on the floor,
And someone called me by my name:
It had become a glimmering girl
With apple blossom in her hair
Who called me by my name and ran
And faded through the brightening air.

Though I am old with wandering
Through hollow lands and hilly lands,
I will find out where she has gone,
And kiss her lips and take her hands;
And walk among long dappled grass,
And pluck till time and times are done,
The silver apples of the moon,
The golden apples of the sun.
```

Text from [The Song of Wandering Aengus — Wikisource](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Song_of_Wandering_Aengus). Public domain in the US (Collected in The Wind Among the Reeds in 1899; works first published in the United States by 1930 are public domain.).

## Summary

The speaker goes into a hazel wood, makes a simple fishing rod, and catches a silver trout. When he turns from the fire, the trout has become a glimmering girl who calls his name and disappears.

Now old from wandering, he remains certain that he will find her. His imagined reunion joins physical intimacy with a harvest of the moon's silver apples and the sun's golden apples.

## Meaning and interpretation

The poem treats desire as both an interruption and a life direction. A mysterious impulse sends the speaker into the woods, and the fish's transformation gives that impulse a face. Because the girl vanishes almost as soon as she appears, the speaker spends his life pursuing an ideal shaped by one fleeting vision.

The ending does not settle whether the search is futile or spiritually sustaining. The silver and golden apples suggest a perfected, imaginative realm: the speaker may be seeking a person, a supernatural figure, or the beauty and creative vision that art can preserve. His certainty that he will find her keeps hope alive while also revealing the persistence of obsession.

## Themes

### Longing and unattainable desire

The speaker's encounter lasts only a moment, but it governs the rest of his life. His wandering shows how an ideal can become more powerful precisely because it remains out of reach.

### Myth and transformation

An ordinary trout becomes a named, shining girl, moving the poem from practical fishing into mythic vision. Yeats gives the ancient figure of Aengus a personal quest rather than presenting a complete traditional legend.

### Time, age, and eternity

The speaker is already old, yet his future verbs remain forceful: he will find, kiss, take, walk, and pluck. Mortal aging is set against the repeated promise of “time and times” and the enduring images of moon and sun.

## Form and meter

The poem has three eight-line stanzas. Each stanza uses alternating end-rhymes, with some looseness in the opening pairings, while repeated conjunctions and parallel phrasing create a ballad-like forward motion.

Its underlying movement is mostly iambic tetrameter, four rising beats per line, though Yeats varies the rhythm with extra syllables, substitutions, pauses, and longer compound phrases. The conversational meter lets the supernatural event arrive without a change in the speaker's plain narrative voice.

The poem's syntax also develops across the stanzas: practical actions lead to sudden transformation, then to a long vow projected into the future. The final stanza's repeated “And” makes the search feel continuous and unfinished.

## Literary devices

### Symbolism

> The silver apples of the moon,

The silver and golden apples suggest perfected beauty, celestial mystery, and a harvest that cannot be gathered in ordinary human time. Their pairing of moon and sun gives the speaker's desired world a total, almost eternal scale.

### Transformation

> It had become a glimmering girl

The trout's sudden change turns a small fishing scene into a supernatural encounter. The transformation also makes desire unstable: what the speaker catches is not what he finally wants.

### Sensory imagery

> With apple blossom in her hair

The poem combines touch, color, light, and natural fragrance in its images of the girl and the landscape. This sensory richness makes the brief vision feel vivid enough to justify a lifetime of memory.

### Repetition and parallelism

> Who called me by my name and ran

Repeated structures such as “called me by my name” and the sequence “kiss,” “take,” “walk,” and “pluck” connect recognition, pursuit, and imagined reunion. The syntax keeps the speaker moving toward an event that never occurs within the poem.

## Historical context

The poem was first printed in 1897 under the title “A Mad Song” and was collected under its familiar title in The Wind Among the Reeds in 1899. The Poetry Foundation identifies its source collection and marks the poem public domain.

Yeats wrote within a sustained interest in Irish folklore, mythology, and occult or visionary experience. LitCharts describes the speaker as Aengus, an Irish mythological god associated with youth, love, and poetic inspiration, while also noting that Yeats drew on both Irish tradition and a Greek folk song.

The poem adapts myth rather than simply retelling a single legend. Its Aengus is an aging wanderer whose encounter with a mysterious girl turns mythic identity into a human story of memory, pursuit, and frustrated desire.

## What critics say

> “a dramatic monologue about burning and thwarted passion”
>
> — [LitCharts](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/william-butler-yeats/the-song-of-wandering-aengus)

> “As a kind of miniature fable, the poem suggests how unrequited love—or any other unattainable dream—can both exhaust a person's energies and nourish a person's imagination.”
>
> — [LitCharts](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/william-butler-yeats/the-song-of-wandering-aengus)

> “The Song of Wandering Aengus’ by William Butler Yeats describes Aengus’ quest to find a girl he once saw in his youth.”
>
> — Emma Baldwin, [Poem Analysis](https://poemanalysis.com/william-butler-yeats/the-song-of-wandering-aengus/)

## Common questions

### What is the meaning of The Song of Wandering Aengus?

The poem presents a fleeting supernatural encounter as the source of a lifelong search. The girl can be read as lost love, an unattainable ideal, or a vision of beauty and creative inspiration.

### What are the main themes in The Song of Wandering Aengus?

Its main themes include longing, myth and transformation, the tension between aging and eternity, and the way an imagined ideal can shape an entire life.

### What meter does The Song of Wandering Aengus use?

The poem is mostly written in iambic tetrameter, with four main rising beats per line. Yeats varies the pattern to preserve a natural, songlike speaking voice.

### Who is Aengus in the poem?

Aengus is a figure from Irish mythology associated with youth, love, and poetic inspiration. Yeats uses him as the speaker of a personal, visionary story rather than retelling one myth in full.

## References

- [The Song of Wandering Aengus — full poem](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Song_of_Wandering_Aengus) — Wikisource

- [The Song of Wandering Aengus — Poetry Foundation](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/55687/the-song-of-wandering-aengus) — The Poetry Foundation

- [The Song of Wandering Aengus — LitCharts](https://www.litcharts.com/poetry/william-butler-yeats/the-song-of-wandering-aengus) — LitCharts

- [The Song of Wandering Aengus — Poem Analysis](https://poemanalysis.com/william-butler-yeats/the-song-of-wandering-aengus/) — Poem Analysis

# The Tyger analysis

The Tyger — William Blake (1794)

This analysis of William Blake’s “The Tyger” explains how its relentless questions, forge imagery, and contrast with “The Lamb” make creation both beautiful and frightening.

## The poem

```
Tyger Tyger, burning bright,
In the forests of the night;
What immortal hand or eye,
Could frame thy fearful symmetry?

In what distant deeps or skies.
Burnt the fire of thine eyes?
On what wings dare he aspire?
What the hand, dare seize the fire?

And what shoulder, & what art,
Could twist the sinews of thy heart?
And when thy heart began to beat.
What dread hand? & what dread feet?

What the hammer? what the chain,
In what furnace was thy brain?
What the anvil? what dread grasp.
Dare its deadly terrors clasp?

When the stars threw down their spears
And water'd heaven with their tears:
Did he smile his work to see?
Did he who made the Lamb make thee?

Tyger Tyger, burning bright,
In the forests of the night:
What immortal hand or eye,
Dare frame thy fearful symmetry?
```

Text from [The Tyger](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/43687/the-tyger). Public domain in the US (First published in Songs of Experience in 1794; William Blake died in 1827, so the poem is public domain in the United States.).

## Summary

The speaker addresses the mysterious maker of a tiger whose beauty and violence are inseparable. Each stanza intensifies the question of how such a creature could be designed.

The poem never answers its questions. Its final stanza repeats the opening but changes “Could” to “Dare,” shifting attention from the creator’s ability to the audacity of making something so fearsome.

## Meaning and interpretation

The Tyger is not simply a symbol of evil. Its “fearful symmetry” joins order and terror, while the repeated questions leave its moral meaning unresolved. Blake makes uncertainty part of the poem’s subject.

The poem’s central theological problem is whether the same creator could make both the gentle Lamb and the dangerous Tyger. Rather than choosing one over the other, Blake places innocence and experience in a tense, mutually revealing relationship.

## Themes

### Creation and divine mystery

The speaker can imagine the Tyger’s design but cannot identify or understand its maker. The unanswered questions preserve creation as something larger than human explanation.

### Beauty and terror

“Burning bright” and “fearful symmetry” make the creature visually compelling, but the poem’s fire, dread, and deadly terrors keep admiration close to fear.

### Innocence and experience

The question “Did he who made the Lamb make thee?” directly connects this poem with “The Lamb.” Their different tones and creatures test whether a complete creation can contain both gentleness and force.

## Form and meter

The poem has six quatrains and is commonly read as trochaic tetrameter, often catalectic: four falling rhythmic units with the final unstressed syllable omitted. The hammering beat suits the forge imagery and the speaker’s urgency.

Most stanzas use rhyming couplets, though “eye” and “symmetry” can sound like a slant rhyme to modern readers. The repeated opening and closing stanzas create a circular structure, while “Could” becoming “Dare” marks the poem’s crucial change.

Nearly every line belongs to a question. The interrogative structure refuses a settled explanation and makes the reader experience the same uncertainty as the speaker.

## Literary devices

### Rhetorical questions

> What immortal hand or eye, / Could frame thy fearful symmetry?

The poem accumulates questions without providing answers. This turns uncertainty from a gap in the argument into its central formal effect.

### Forge imagery

> What the hammer? what the chain, / In what furnace was thy brain?

Hammer, chain, furnace, and anvil recast the creator as a laboring blacksmith. Creation becomes physical, forceful work rather than distant abstraction.

### Paradox

> Could frame thy fearful symmetry?

“Symmetry” suggests order and beauty, while “fearful” suggests danger. The paired terms hold attraction and terror together in one image.

### Repetition and variation

> Could frame thy fearful symmetry? ... Dare frame thy fearful symmetry?

The final stanza echoes the first almost exactly. The change from “Could” to “Dare” turns a question of capacity into a question of moral nerve.

## Historical context

Blake published “The Tyger” in Songs of Experience in 1794, the companion half of Songs of Innocence and of Experience. The collection’s subtitle presents the poems as “Two Contrary States of the Human Soul.”

Blake produced his books through illuminated printing, combining etched text and images and hand-colouring copies. The poem’s image of a maker working with fire and tools therefore resonates with Blake’s own identity as a poet, engraver, and visual artist.

The title’s spelling, “Tyger,” is retained from Blake’s text and should not be modernized to “Tiger.”

## What critics say

> “The poem is built entirely from questions. Thirteen of them, by most counts, and not one receives an answer.”
>
> — Poetry Lovers’ Page editors, [Poetry Lovers’ Page](https://www.poetryloverspage.com/poets/blake/tiger/literary-analysis)

> “God is thus ‘reduced’ to the status of an artisan or skilled craftsman.”
>
> — Oliver Tearle, [Interesting Literature](https://interestingliterature.com/2023/04/blake-tyger-symbolism-imagery/)

> “Because we cannot provide definite answers to the questions the speaker poses, there is something mysterious about the Tyger – so that is another thing it represents: something unknown, and perhaps unknowable.”
>
> — Oliver Tearle, [Interesting Literature](https://interestingliterature.com/2023/04/blake-tyger-symbolism-imagery/)

## Common questions

### What is the main meaning of “The Tyger”?

The poem asks how a creator could make something that is both beautiful and terrifying. It does not resolve the question, presenting mystery and contradiction as central to creation.

### What does the Tyger symbolize?

The Tyger can symbolize fierce energy, danger, sublime power, or the difficult aspects of creation. Blake’s questions keep its meaning open rather than reducing it to simple evil.

### How does “The Tyger” contrast with “The Lamb”?

“The Lamb” asks who made the lamb and answers with childlike confidence. “The Tyger” asks whether the same maker created both animals and leaves the question unanswered, placing innocence beside experience.

### What is the poem’s meter?

The poem is commonly scanned as trochaic tetrameter, often with catalectic lines. Its falling, hammer-like rhythm reinforces the forge imagery and the repeated questioning.

### Why does Blake use forge imagery?

The hammer, chain, furnace, and anvil make creation seem physical and laborious. They present the maker as a powerful artisan who must shape dangerous energy into a living form.

## References

- [Poem text and 1794 publication credit](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/43687/the-tyger) — Poetry Foundation

- [Public-domain text and collection context](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Songs_of_Innocence_and_of_Experience_(1826)/Songs_of_Experience/The_Tyger) — Wikisource

- [Symbolism and forge imagery](https://interestingliterature.com/2023/04/blake-tyger-symbolism-imagery/) — Interesting Literature

## Open the editor

Write with this poem’s meter in the editor: https://lyriic.com/write
